title: Rising from the valley: a new sustainable woodland centre takes shape at Yarner Wood

content.content: By Chris Harbut, Reserve Manager, Devon National Nature Reserves

Tucked into a steep-sided Dartmoor valley, a new woodland centre is taking shape at Yarner Wood, built almost entirely from timber grown in the surrounding landscape. In this post, we share how the building is coming together, from the Douglas fir frame to the cedar cladding still to come. We also explain how sustainability has shaped every decision, including the off-grid power and water systems, and how we hope the centre will welcome schools, community groups and partners when it opens at the end of the year.

If you've visited Yarner Wood recently, you may have noticed something new rising among the trees. Tucked into this steep-sided Dartmoor valley, within the East Dartmoor National Nature Reserve (NNR), a new woodland centre is taking shape. One built almost entirely from timber sourced from the surrounding landscape. We wanted to share the story of how it's coming together, and why sustainability is at the very heart of this project.

Construction of this new, purpose-built facility, will replace the previous woodland centre. Work began earlier this year, and since then it's been a hive of activity here at Yarner. Following the initial site clearance and logistics work, the timber frame has been erected, the roof is on, windows are being installed, and cladding is being put on.

This is no standard facility, but a considered response to its unique landscape setting, with generous natural light and a strong sense of place designed to keep visitors connected to the woodland around them at every turn.
A building made from the woodland it sits within

The timber is the star of this project. The building's frame, now proudly standing tall, is built from beams crafted from Douglas fir donated by the Woodland Trust. The timber was sourced from within the NNR, from Plantations on Ancient Woodland Sites (PAWS). This is ongoing woodland restoration work that is transitioning conifer plantations on ancient woodland sites back to native deciduous woodland and temperate rainforest. Use of this material directly links the building to ongoing landscape restoration efforts.

That story will continue over the coming weeks. Once the windows are fitted, exterior cladding will go on, predominantly using western red cedar, also supplied by the Woodland Trust. This timber is naturally durable and oily, requiring minimal treatment to stay weatherproof, further reducing the building's long-term environmental impact and maintenance needs.
Sustainability at the core
As the building sits entirely within the NNR , sustainability and environmental sensitivity have shaped every part of the project.

The facility will operate fully off-grid. Water will be supplied through rainwater harvesting and, where appropriate, the adjacent stream. Solar panels will feed a substantial battery storage system, with approximately 30 kVA of capacity, significantly reducing reliance on fossil fuels and allowing the building to run silently for much of the year.

Due to the building's location in a steep-sided, wooded Dartmoor valley, power generation can be limited during periods of low sunlight, particularly in winter. As a result, a generator will remain part of the energy system, although it has been relocated further from the building and will be used far less frequently. The battery system ensures that low-level power demands, such as lighting, no longer require the generator to run continuously. During summer months, generator use is unlikely to be needed.

Heating will be provided primarily by a gasification boiler rather than electric systems. Combined with exceptionally high levels of insulation, this means the building will need very little energy input to stay comfortable year-round. While not formally certified as a passive building, it has been designed to perform close to passive standards within practical and budgetary constraints.
Looking ahead
Once finished, the new centre will play a key role in supporting engagement, events and activities, having been designed specifically to enable and promote this kind of activity.

The old woodland centre has long been a hub for the local community, with schools, universities and student nurses among those who have used the space over the years. We want to build on that success.
As the new centre takes shape, we're keen to work with local organisations, partners across the sector, and community groups to explore additional uses and reach new people.

If you'd like to be part of that conversation we'd love to hear from you, so do get in touch. Keep an eye on the East Dartmoor NNR social channels for more updates as the building work heads towards completion at the end of the year.

title: How infrastructure bodies help charities navigate today's risks

content.content: Our recent Charity Sector Risk Assessment underlined how charities continue to deliver extraordinary impact for the communities they serve, but that they are doing so against a backdrop of considerable pressures.
Our analysis shows that while overall sector income and expenditure both grew in 2024, the financial margin across the sector has not yet recovered to pre-pandemic levels.

Financial pressure understandably, can lead to governance challenges. In the past year, we saw a 57% increase in cases involving internal disputes within charities, covering matters such as trustee elections and disagreements over land or property. Our engagement with the sector suggests that this rise is partly a consequence of the difficult decisions charities are having to make in response to financial strain, compounded by wider societal tensions.
The role of infrastructure bodies

While the Commission provides guidance to help trustees understand their duties, we can’t directly solve the financial and operational challenges charities face day to day. This is where infrastructure and umbrella bodies can play a vital role, offering practical advice and support that complements our regulatory guidance.
We spoke to Liz Lowther, Chief Executive Officer of the Association of Chairs and asked her about navigating this challenging environment while helping others do the same.
Tell us a little about your organisation

AoC: All charities are led by trustees – but these leaders aren’t always given the support, training, and development they need to fulfil their crucial volunteer roles. That’s why we exist. We champion and support chairs and trustees so they can be the best leaders they can be. Strong, effective boards make better collective decisions, maximising their charity’s resilience and social impact. With our specialist training, resources, support services and our community, we make sure chairs and trustees have the confidence and knowledge they need to lead their charities well.
Can you give us a practical example of how you’ve helped a charity fulfil its mission more effectively in recent months?

AoC: With our unique community and understanding of the challenges facing chairs and trustees, we are able to support them when the going gets tough. This is particularly helpful for smaller charities (60% of our members have a turnover below £1m), which do not have funds to spare on expensive advice or legal support. One charity we helped recently was facing a raft of issues related to serious complaints, safeguarding issues, sudden managerial exits and problems with their organisational culture. Their chair contacted us for advice on how to tackle these, and to ensure they were acting in line with their legal responsibilities. Through our experienced chair network and access to our mentoring services, they received guidance and help to come up with an action plan to address all the concerns. This enabled the board to work more effectively with the senior leadership team to resolve the challenges and refocus on the charity’s mission.
Are there are common misunderstandings about infrastructure bodies?

AoC: Some people might think that infrastructure organisations are removed from the day-to-day challenges that other charities face, or may see them as less valuable than frontline organisations. But infrastructure plays an essential role in helping charities be more resilient and effective, with a huge multiplier effect. It’s a really cost-effective way for charities to access the support and connections they need. AoC is itself a small charity, and our membership fees contribute towards the delivery of our services. We also provide bursaries, and free events and resources wherever possible, recognising that many who need the support may not otherwise be able to access it.
What is the biggest challenge facing infrastructure bodies right now?

AoC: As recent high-profile closures have shown, infrastructure organisations are facing increased financial pressures at the same time as sector needs have grown and become more complex. Funding for infrastructure has been shrinking for some time. Charities are having to make difficult decisions about where to allocate scarce resources while faced with increasing costs, and funding for memberships, training and development are often among the first to be cut. This is particularly true when it comes to board development - the Charity Commission and Pro Bono Economic's  2025 national trustee survey found that only 48% felt confident they had access to the training needed to fulfil their role. This is a challenge for infrastructure but also for effective sector leadership and governance. As infrastructure, our role in providing guidance and advocacy has never been more critical, and the support networks we provide never more needed.
Forging a stronger sector

Unfortunately, infrastructure bodies are not insulated from the financial pressures affecting the wider sector. We had been working with the Directory of Social Change on a contribution to this blog, but sadly it recently announced that it had appointed an insolvency practitioner to oversee its closure. Reach Volunteering, also shared its planned closure in September but by the end of that month, it had reversed the decision after receiving “unprecedented” support from funders.

The sector's resilience depends not only on individual charities managing their own risks well, but on a strong and sustainable network of support around them. While the extent of engagement with infrastructure bodies is a matter for individual charities to determine in their own context, at sector level the Commission sees huge value in their continuing role.

Julia Unwin, Charity Commission Chair, described them in her recent speech at our Annual Public Meeting as “the rich web of organisations that provide support, bring organisations together, provide the scaffolding that keeps charities running effectively and efficiently.”

These bodies are uniquely placed to offer peer support to charity leaders, share practical advice and resources to reduce the need for charities to pay for professional advice and to advocate for the sector across government and beyond. The Commission will continue to engage with infrastructure bodies as they help charities manage a changing landscape in the months and years ahead.
Our full Charity Sector Risk Assessment 2026, along with our related guidance for trustees, is available on GOV.UK.

title: MOT horror stories: helping your customers keep vehicles roadworthy

content.content: A badly damaged tyre. A suspension arm almost rusted through. For MOT testers, these Halloween horror stories are a reminder of the defects you encounter and the value of your expertise.

Thank you to the garages and testers who sent in photographs. This year, we’re sharing them on social media and with journalists to remind motorists why maintenance matters between MOTs, and when to seek professional advice from their local garage.
Shorn of the tread
This badly damaged tyre provides a starting point for a conversation with customers about regular tyre checks.
We know you’ll always remind customers to look for damage such as cuts, bulges and cracks, and seek professional advice if concerned.
It’s key to also encourage customers to check the whole tyre for wear and damage, and the condition of any spare.
Some drivers will also benefit from a reminder that tyre pressures should follow the vehicle manufacturer’s recommendations in the handbook or on the vehicle.
A real dead springer
A tester found this Ford Ka’s suspension arm severely corroded and almost snapped off.

You may get an opportunity to encourage customers to seek your professional advice if their vehicle reacts differently to bumps or makes unusual noises before the next MOT. Explaining MOT advisories clearly and encouraging timely action rather than waiting for the next test.
Unidentified floating object
An object hanging from the roof of this van obstructed the driver’s view.
We know you’ll remind customers to keep their windscreen and view of the road and mirrors clear, and remove obstructions before driving – not just before the MOT.
It’s a good opportunity to also encourage customers to check that wipers and washers clear the windscreen effectively.
A cautionary tale

You can play a key role in helping customers understand that a valid MOT is not a guarantee of roadworthiness for the year. Your explanation of defects and advisories can help them act before problems worsen.

What helps you explain defects and advisories to customers? Share your practical advice and testing experiences in the comments.
Thank you for your work helping keep vehicles roadworthy – this Halloween and throughout the year.

title: Radioactivity in food and the environment - our 2025 report.

content.content: Becca Williams and Rob Dean
We’ve published our annual report about radioactivity in food and the environment (RIFE) The RIFE 31 report sets out the findings of monitoring carried out in 2025.

In this blog, the Environment Agency’s radiological monitoring and assessment specialists Becca Williams and Rob Dean share the headlines from this year’s monitoring and assessment work and reveal how artificial radioactivity gets into the environment.
Headlines
Radioactivity in food and the environment is safe.

Overall, between 2024 and 2025 there were no major changes to the radioactivity measured in food and the environment and the public’s exposure to radiation from sites permitted by the Environment Agency was well below legal limits.
Our radiological monitoring team

The Environment Agency’s radiological monitoring team work remotely in different parts of England. We manage several different monitoring programmes that measure radioactivity in the environment and support the production of the annual Radioactivity in Food and the Environment (RIFE) report. We also provide radiological assessment advice to ensure protection of the environment and the public from impacts of radioactive discharges.
Independent monitoring programmes

We run several different radioactivity monitoring programmes that are independent of the nuclear industry in England and Wales. We monitor many different samples including air, rainwater and sources of drinking water. We also monitor grass and seaweed and our partner organisation monitors different food types such as milk.
The results of all our programmes are published annually in the RIFE report. The programmes:
We use specialist laboratories to carry out the analysis and measurements and again this year’s RIFE report contains over 10,000 pieces of analysis and measurements.
How do artificial sources of radioactivity get into the environment?

Radioactivity is all around us. It occurs naturally in the Earth’s crust and in most of our homes, in food we eat, water we drink and the air we breathe. We are also exposed to artificial sources of radioactivity, such as those used in medical settings, nuclear power stations and from nuclear weapons testing fallout and historic nuclear incidents.

It’s a legal requirement to make sure the amount of artificial radioactivity that people are exposed to from discharges is kept within a safe limit. The requirements for regulating public exposure from the disposal of radioactive waste in England and Wales are set out in the Environmental Permitting (England and Wales) Regulations 2016 (as amended) which transposes the requirements of the Basic Safety Standard Directive.

If any organisation in England, such as a nuclear power station operator, university research laboratory or hospital, wants to use radioactive substances they must have a permit from the Environment Agency. These environmental permits contain strict conditions (rules) that they must always follow. We also set specific limits on what they are allowed to release when carrying out certain activities.

Before we issue a permit we assess how discharges of radioactivity will affect humans, plants and animals on land and in rivers and marine environments. The methodology and system used by our scientists to assess radiation doses to people and wildlife is published on gov.uk.
Our nuclear regulators carry out checks to make sure that operators do not release radioactivity above the limits set in their permit conditions.
But it’s worth emphasising, as the diagram below shows, only a small percentage of all radioactivity in the environment is artificial. Most is naturally occurring.
How we assess exposure to radiation
Our monitoring programmes help us to understand the levels of radioactivity in food and the environment.

We use habit surveys to investigate the behaviour and diet of people living near nuclear sites to assess their exposure to radiation. Experts conduct interviews with members of the public, focussing on identifying those who are most likely to be exposed to radiation. We use this data alongside environmental monitoring data to estimate doses of radiation the public is exposed to. These estimated doses are reported annually in our RIFE report.
Habit surveys were published this year for Sellafield (Cumbria), Barrow (Cumbria) and Sizewell (Suffolk).
More information

We publish information from our monitoring programmes every autumn. You can read this year’s short summary and detailed report on GOV.UK  or look back at previous year’s reports on the National Archives.

We’ll also be sharing the results with communities, local representatives and environmental groups that live near nuclear sites. You can read our reports to site stakeholder groups or attend ‘meet the regulator meetings’ in some areas.
If you have any questions about the report please email us: nuclear@environment-agency.gov.uk.

title: Helping more people off the streets: how AI is improving StreetLink

content.content: StreetLink is a national service in England and Wales that helps members of the public share concerns about someone sleeping rough so that local outreach teams can respond. It is funded by the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government (MHCLG) with delivery partner Home Connections responsible for delivering the service.
Every StreetLink alert has the potential to change someone's day.
When a member of the public spots someone sleeping rough and reports this through StreetLink by submitting an alert, outreach teams rely on the information provided to locate them and offer support.

The quality of that information matters, so a detailed description of the location, such as descriptions of landmarks and distinguishing features, can significantly improve the outreach team’s success in locating the person.
An AI pilot with transformative impact

Over the past several weeks, colleagues from MHCLG’s Homelessness and Rough Sleeping Directorate have been working with Home Connections on a pilot project with 10 local authorities to explore whether AI technology could enhance the service in a practical, responsible and user-centred way.

The project was backed by MHCLG’s Local AI team, which provided funding and support, working closely with the StreetLink team as the project developed. Local AI acted as a sounding board, shared AI and product expertise, and brought learning from similar work across local government. This helped explore different approaches and shape the pilot.
The pilot had an immediate, transformative impact, halving the number of failed outreach attempts caused by poor descriptive data – dropping from 36% to 18%.

The significance of this outcome is already being recognised. Vicky Sterrett, contract manager for StreetLink in the Homelessness and Rough Sleeping Directorate, recently won the inaugural Cabinet Secretary’s AI Innovation Award for her work on the project.
In the next sections, we’ve invited Sharon Fernando from Home Connections to share the lessons and impact of the pilot. Here’s what Sharon said:

“From my experience, the AI features introduced during the pilot have made a noticeable improvement to the quality of the referrals we receive in Newport. One of the most useful additions has been the prompt encouraging people to provide a What3Words location. This has made it much easier for our team to find exact locations, particularly where there isn't a formal address or where someone is sleeping in a less obvious spot. Having that level of accuracy saves time and makes outreach visits more effective. Overall, I feel the AI pilot has improved the consistency and quality of information we receive through StreetLink. The referrals are more actionable, which ultimately helps us provide a better and more responsive service to people sleeping rough.” Isabel Young, Rough Sleeper Support Officer, Newport

“StreetLink exists to help people sleeping rough get support as quickly as possible. The pilot has shown that by improving the quality of information we receive, we can help outreach teams locate people more effectively and reduce missed opportunities for support. The results demonstrate that carefully designed AI can improve both the user experience and service outcomes, helping to ensure that more people receive the support they need.” Kam Basra, Deputy Chief Executive, Home Connections
What happens next
The outcomes of the pilot are clear – improvements are saving time and making the service more efficient. The full rollout is now live on the service across England and Wales.
This is particularly important as we all work together to support the Prime Minister's ambition of ensuring everyone sleeping rough has a route off the streets by Christmas.

The team will continue to work closely with local authorities, outreach providers and partners to ensure the solution fits naturally within existing workflows while continuing to improve the quality of information received through StreetLink.

As we build on the lessons from this pilot, we'll continue to ensure technology supports – not replaces – the people at the heart of StreetLink. By combining innovation with frontline expertise, we hope to make it easier for outreach teams to connect with people sleeping rough and help them access the support they need.
Recognition for the team

We are delighted that Vicky Sterrett, StreetLink contract manager in the Homelessness and Rough Sleeping Directorate, recently won the inaugural Cabinet Secretary’s AI Innovation Award for her important work on the pilot.
The award recognised the project’s practical impact, ingenuity and focus on using AI to make public services simpler, better and faster.

“It's easy to get excited about new technology, but for me the question is always: will this actually help people or meet the problem at hand, and will it make things easier for the teams using it? As contract manager for StreetLink, I’m pleased to see such strong evidence of the difference this pilot has made. The AI features helped users provide more detailed and useful information, resulting in better-quality alerts and improved outcomes for outreach teams. Ultimately, that means a greater chance of connecting people sleeping rough with the support they need.” Vicky Sterrett

“This project is a brilliant example of AI being used to solve a real problem and make a tangible difference. The StreetLink team and Home Connections have done a fantastic job turning innovation into practical impact, and their award is thoroughly deserved. This is exactly the kind of work we want to support through Local AI.” Sam Selmon, Head of Product, Local AI

This work has been a genuine team effort. Thank you to all colleagues across participating local authorities, Home Connections and the wider StreetLink partnership who helped design, test, improve and deliver the pilot. Their expertise and commitment have been central to its success.
To find out more about StreetLink, get in touch with patrick.duce@communities.gov.uk.
If you’re interested in the work of Local AI, read about our recent projects or contact LocalAI@communities.gov.uk.

title: What can we learn from Europe about regulatory scrutiny?

content.content: I recently attended the annual conference of the European Regulatory Scrutiny Board (RSB) in Brussels, where they discuss the work of the RSB and its Annual Report.

The report presents a challenging picture of the quality of European Commission assessments at first submitted – 56% of impact assessments and 41% of evaluations and fitness checks received a negative opinion and showed the improvement to the quality of assessments from going through RSB review.
The areas highlighted as particularly weak were:
There are a lot of similarities between the work of the RSB and the Regulatory Policy Committee (RPC):
However there are important differences – here are a few, with my thoughts added.

The RSB holds ‘upstream meetings’ with the Commission services to offer informal targeted advice at an early stage of the preparation of the impact assessment (IA) or evaluation to advise on the intervention logic and chosen methodology for assessing costs and benefits and guide the development of the IA.

While the RPC secretariat has informal meetings with department policy teams, I can see the advantage of informally involving the RPC committee at an earlier stage in policy making. This would support the development of IAs and ensure that our views on the clarity of policy objectives, rationale for intervention and choice of preferred policy option are taken on board at a point at which they can actually influence the IA development.

Unlike the RPC’s role which is purely advisory - ministers can (and sometimes do) take forward legislation where the IA has been deemed ‘not fit for purpose’; if the RSB rates the IA as negative, it must be resubmitted for a second opinion, if it receives a second negative opinion the Commissioner for Economy and Productivity then decides whether and in what form it can proceed.

I actually think that our approach is preferable – in my opinion, it is not for an arm’s-length body like the RPC to block the development of policy of the democratically elected government. However we play an important role in informing parliamentarians and other stakeholders of the quality of the evidence underpinning legislative proposals – good or bad.

Interestingly, one of the RSB’s quality components is ‘readability and clarity’, as part of this it recommends (subject to derogation) a maximum assessment length – 40 pages for IAs and 50 pages for evaluations.

While it would be difficult to keep to such a limit for large multi-part measures (the Employment Rights Bill IA included 23 separate IAs – one for each of the different elements of the bill), I can see the advantages of recommended page limits that encourage departments to set out their analysis concisely and that facilitate the use of IAs by policy-makers and other stakeholders.

The EU process places far more emphasis on feeding through the results of evaluations into future policy development than does the British approach. I think this is a clear gap in our system that we could learn from. I wrote about this recently in our blog – the EU approach demonstrates that feeding the results of post-implementation reviews into policy development can be effectively integrated in a coherent regulatory framework.

title: Part 3: From Ambition to Action: Protecting the UK’s Blue Belt

content.content: In 2016, only around 5% of the world's oceans were formally protected through designated MPAs, and many of those lacked the resources, science and management needed to deliver effective protection. It was against this backdrop that the UK Government launched the Blue Belt Programme, a transformative commitment to marine conservation across the UK Overseas Territories.

Initially focused on supporting UK Overseas Territories that had, or wished to establish, large-scale MPAs, the Programme sought to move beyond simple designation and ensure that protected areas were underpinned by robust science, effective management and long-term protection.

Today, Blue Belt supports the protection and sustainable management of more than 4 million km² of marine environment across the UK Overseas Territories, making it one of the world's most comprehensive marine conservation initiatives. It focuses on three strategic themes: nature, climate and people.

For nature, the Programme supports scientific research, biodiversity monitoring and ecosystem assessments that improve our understanding of marine species and habitats. This includes large-scale surveys, long-term monitoring programmes and initiatives such as the Global Ocean Wildlife Analysis Network (GOWAN), helping Territories make evidence-based management decisions. Compliance and enforcement is achieved through daily monitoring of activities, minimising illegal, unregulated and unreported fishing, as well as reducing potential marine pollution events. Together, these measures have helped UK Overseas Territories gain international recognition for effective marine protection, including prestigious Blue Park Awards.

For climate, Blue Belt helps Territories protect and manage marine ecosystems that support climate resilience and help communities adapt to environmental change, such as strengthening storms, sea level rise and associated coastal flooding and erosion.

For people, the Programme supports the development of management plans, legislation and governance frameworks that reflect each Territory's unique environmental, social and cultural needs. It invests in training, equipment and local capacity, while supporting stakeholder engagement, education and outreach activities that help communities understand the purpose and benefits of MPAs. By ensuring decisions are informed by local knowledge and community voices, Blue Belt promotes equitable, inclusive and locally led marine management.

Ultimately, the Blue Belt Programme helps turn marine protection from a line on a map into meaningful action, delivering lasting benefits for nature, climate and people. You can discover the full extent of the Programme's support in the 10-year impact report .
Case study: South Georgia & the South Sandwich Islands renew their MPA management plan

In the Southern Ocean, South Georgia & the South Sandwich Islands lie isolated, unimaginably remote from any other land. And yet, surrounding these islands of ice and rock is an MPA so large it accounts for over 5% of global MPA coverage.

Established in 2012, the MPA is one of the most ecologically significant, biodiverse and productive marine conservation zones in the world. Within its 1.24 million km² boundaries are crucial polar habitats supporting whales, seals and five species of penguin, sustained by vast krill stocks that underpin the majority of the Southern Ocean food web. The MPA protects important foraging grounds for migratory whales and seabirds, while on the seafloor, cold-water corals form otherworldly habitats deep below the surface.

South Georgia & the South Sandwich Islands was one of the first large-scale MPAs globally to commit to regular reviews from the outset. The Blue Belt Programme supported the Government of South Georgia & the South Sandwich Islands with its first five-year review in 2017 to 2018, which led to strengthened protections, including expanded no-take zones, seasonal closures to safeguard breeding wildlife, and a ban on the carriage of heavy fuel oil.

Between 2024 and 2025, the MPA underwent its second five-yearly review. At the start of 2026, South Georgia & the South Sandwich Islands published their reviewed MPA management plan, a culmination of five years of scientific evidence and stakeholder insights, resulting in a strengthened roadmap securing the long-term protection of this globally significant marine environment.

In a world of increasing environmental threats, from climate change to pollution and overfishing, South Georgia & the South Sandwich Islands stand as a beacon of hope. By undertaking comprehensive reviews every five years, the MPA remains effective and responsive to emerging scientific evidence and environmental change. title: Buried Alive: A Patent Solution

content.content: It's Halloween, so the fleeting worry of being buried alive may have crossed your mind – though a few centuries ago, you would have had far greater reason to be concerned. With limited medical knowledge and no safeguards to protect the unfortunate soul, premature burial was a very real possibility.

There are accounts from as early as the 14th century of people being buried alive. One medieval tale tells how Philosopher John Duns Scotus was found outside his coffin with horrifying wounds to his hands, suggesting he had clawed his way out. Though the reliability of the story is doubtful, there have been others….

Alice Blunden managed it twice! The blood curdling tale took place in 17th century Basingstoke where Alice fell unconscious after drinking a large amount of poppy tea. The tea made from dried, unwashed seed pods would have contained the powerful sedatives morphine and codeine.

Her family were unable to revive her whilst a doctor, after holding a mirror to her nose and mouth, pronounced her dead. She was quickly buried but two days after this, children playing near the grave heard muffled noises and screams. Their schoolmaster, not believing the children, delayed investigation for a day and once he suspected Alice was still alive, it took another day to exhume her.

In a dark turn, after exhuming Alice her family decided she was so close to death, that she should be returned to her grave. According to the Basingstoke gazette, ‘The next morning on opening the coffin once more, it was discovered that Mrs Blunden had woke, torn her grave clothes, scratched at her body and face, and was covered in blood. And overnight she had died.’
These horrifying real-life accounts didn't just haunt families—they captured the imagination of writers and inventors alike.
Stoking the fear

Writers capitalised on people’s fears with stories like Edgar Allan Poe's 1844 "Premature Burial," where the narrator, consumed by fear of being buried alive, takes extreme precautions in modifying his tomb:
Whether Poe inspired future innovation remains unclear, but his story did precede a creepy category of invention – the coffin alarm.
Coffin Alarms
Coffin alarms were a series of inventions designed to aid someone, who was buried alive, to escape, breathe and signal for help.
US Patent 81437A , Franz Vester, 1868, for an “Improved Burial-Case”
The patent shows a few features designed to prevent the worst from occuring. An air inlet, ladder and a bell to ring in case the unfortunate person was too weak to climb the ladder.
Patent US268693, John Krichbaum,1882, for a “Device for Indicating Life in Buried Persons”

The device includes two key features: a way to signal movement from inside the coffin and a method for allowing fresh air in. According to the description, if the buried person regains consciousness, they can move their hands to rotate the branches of a T-shaped pipe positioned near them. This movement is visible on an above-ground box, indicating activity inside. Meanwhile, the pipe also allows air to flow passively into the coffin. Once enough time has passed to confirm the person is truly deceased, the device can be removed.
GB191006409A, Emily Violet Blacker, 1911, An Improved Life-saving Coffin whereby the Danger Attending Premature Burial can be Entirely Obviated

This Edwardian safety coffin was designed to prevent premature burial. Before the grave was finally filled in, the coffin was placed in the grave and left accessible. It features a spring-loaded lid connected to the deceased's hands via chains and rings attached to a catch mechanism. If the person revives and makes even the slightest hand movement—such as clenching their fists—this releases the catch and triggers powerful springs that force the lid open, even through up to six inches of covering earth or deodorising material. The coffin is made deeper than usual to allow hand movement and can only be locked from outside with a special key. An optional tube with litmus paper could signal when decomposition had begun. This mechanism would allow the final burying of the coffin to take place once there was no longer any doubt about the person’s condition.
Comfort to the living

With the advance of modern medicine, we can measure brain waves, heartbeat and respiration, so determining whether someone is dead or alive has become more exact. That doesn’t mean the inventions have stopped. They’ve just become more about the experience of death and offering comfort to the living.

Take US patent 9226059B1 granted in 2015 to inventor John Knight for ‘Your music for eternity systems’. The system comprises a solar powered digital music player, which allows both the living as well as the dearly departed to be comforted by music or a recorded message. There is a speaker in the casket and a headset jack on the headstone so you can visit your dead relatives and reminisce with meaningful music.

Similarly US Patent 7765656, granted in 2010 to inventor Jeff Dannenberg for an “Apparatus and Method for Generating Post-Burial Audio Communications in a Burial Casket”. This allows the living to communicate with the dead through audio and music files that are automatically played in accordance with a programmed schedule.
Lessons from the Grave

So, there you have it: from Victorian escape mechanisms to solar-powered sound systems, death has proved surprisingly good for intellectual property. Happy Halloween—and remember, if you're planning your eternal rest, don't forget to include your playlist.

description: It's Halloween, so the fleeting worry of being buried alive may have crossed your mind – though a few centuries ago, you would have had far greater reason to be concerned. With limited medical knowledge and no safeguards to protect the unfortunate soul, premature burial was a very real possibility.

title: Mapping the seabed together: reflections from the second leg of the CSM2026 survey

content.content: While the second leg of CSM2026 concluded in May, the value of the data collected continues to be realised. Elizabeth Davis, Senior Geospatial Information Specialist at the UKHO, reflects on her time aboard the survey vessel and the collaboration that helped deliver environmental, hydrographic and marine heritage investigations.
Building on the first survey leg

When we left Falmouth on Tuesday 5 May for the second leg of CSM2026 and arrived back at the survey site off the north Cornish coast on Wednesday 6 May, the data collected during the first two weeks was already helping us identify where to focus our environmental investigations and where further survey work could add the most value.

During transit to the survey site, the team aboard were introduced to one another and briefed on the goals. The hydrographic objectives for the leg were to complete bathymetric data collection in areas identified during the first leg, while also carrying out wreck investigations and feature checks to support navigational chart updates and marine heritage projects.
From seabed data to environmental evidence

One of the most interesting things I observed on board was how data gathered for hydrographic purposes could also support environmental investigations. Features visible in the bathymetry and backscatter data helped colleagues decide where to collect samples and capture seabed imagery that form the foundation for habitat mapping and environmental monitoring.
This collaborative approach was particularly significant, as it marked the first time the vessel had supported such a diverse range of scientific activities during a single survey.
The scale of activity at the first survey site was impressive. During this leg, scientists carried out:

The grab samples were collected under the remit of the UK Civil Hydrography Programme (CHP) for the Maritime and Coastguard Agency (MCA), and habitat mapping purposes for Centre for Environment, Fisheries and Aquaculture Science (Cefas), Natural England and Joint Nature Conservation Committee (JNCC). Despite each organisation having their own specialisms and objectives, scientists from all departments assisted across the acquisition activities onboard to encourage the sharing of research, analysis and skill development.
When the plan changed…

Midway through the leg, worsening weather meant continuing work at the original survey site was no longer the best option. The decision was made to move to a second site off South Devon, which meant developing new priorities while we were underway.

The possibility of poor weather had been considered during the planning stages, and contingency sites identified. As the vessel travelled to the new site, the team worked together to identify alternative priorities based on equipment capabilities, existing data and shared objectives. The range of expertise on board the RV Cefas Endeavour enabled the team to switch to other valuable activities when plans changed.

The weather did not improve over the following days, so we remained at the second survey site to make the most of the time available. Although conditions limited us to collecting bathymetry and backscatter data, the team adapted by moving to 24-hour multibeam acquisition. This demanded a huge amount of teamwork from everyone on board.
Despite the challenging conditions, the total area surveyed of this second site was 70km², including six further wreck investigations.
Bringing the survey to a close
The RV Cefas Endeavour returned to Falmouth on the evening of Monday 18 May, with the scientific crew disembarking the following morning, marking the end of the survey.

Following the four-week deployment, data was brought back by the respective organisations for further analysis. At the UKHO, the bathymetric data collected as part of the CHP will now be processed to support the UK’s Safety of Life at Sea (SOLAS) obligations and future navigational chart updates.
One survey, many outcomes
While the survey had come to an end, the value of the data gathered was beginning to be realised.

CSM2026 demonstrated how data collected once can support the objectives of multiple organisations. Throughout the survey, hydrographic, environmental and marine heritage investigations were carried out alongside one another, helping maximise the value of time spent at sea.
Over the course of the two survey legs, the team surveyed 410 km² of seabed. To put that into context, this is more than the area of the Isle of Wight.

As the first multi-agency, cross-government seabed mapping survey of its kind, CSM2026 demonstrated how organisations can share resources, knowledge and expertise to build a better understanding of the UK's marine environment.
Find out more about the UK Centre for Seabed Mapping and its work to improve our understanding of the UK’s marine environment.

description: Discover how shared expertise helped maximise the value of data gathered during this year's CSM2026 survey. From collecting seabed samples to adapting to challenging weather, Elizabeth Davis, Senior Geospatial Information Specialist at the UKHO, reflects on her time aboard the cross-government UK CSM survey.

title: Telling DVLA about a health condition just got easier

content.content: If you hold a driving licence, there are times when you'll need to tell DVLA about your health, for example if you develop a condition or need to renew a short-term medical licence.

We know that dealing with a health condition can already be a worrying time. So, we’ve been working to make telling us about a condition, and renewing your licence when medical information is needed, as simple and straightforward as possible.

Our improved online service now allows many more drivers to manage their medical licensing journey online, from telling us about a condition through to renewing their licence. More than 120,000 customers have already used the service, and we've continued to develop it since launch to support more drivers.
More health conditions can be reported online
Previously, only a limited number of health conditions could be reported online. Our service now covers more than 1,600 conditions.
Not every health condition needs to be reported to DVLA, of course. The online service will let you know whether you need to tell us and, if you do, it will guide you through the information we need.

It also means that if you have more than one health condition, you can tell us about them through our online service. And if you're renewing a short-term medical licence, you can notify us about any new conditions at the same time.
A more joined-up service
We’ve also made some important improvements since the service was introduced.
If you’re renewing your driving licence and you’re aged 70 or over, you can now tell us about a health condition when submitting your renewal application online.
We've done the same for customers applying for their first provisional driving licence, creating a more joined-up experience without the need to move between separate services.
The online service is also now available to customers whose driving licence was previously surrendered, revoked or expired, helping more people manage their medical licensing online.
And the whole service is now available in Welsh, providing the same end-to-end service as the English version.
Manage your application through your Driver and vehicles account
The service is connected to your Driver and vehicles account, which means you can save your progress and come back to your application if you need to.
Once you've submitted it, you can also track the progress of your application through your account.

If the photograph on your licence needs renewing, you can do that as part of the same journey too. Around 30% of medical licence renewals require a new photograph, so bringing this into the online service removes another separate step for many customers.
Helping us deal with applications more efficiently
The improvements are not just about making the application easier to complete.

We've introduced automation to speed up the initial application review. When you tell us about a health condition online, it comes directly into our casework systems in a structured format. This helps our caseworkers review the information they need and decide what needs to happen next.

To make a medical licensing decision, we sometimes need further information from customers or healthcare professionals, so not every case can be completed immediately. But making the initial application more straightforward, and giving our caseworkers better information from the outset, helps us deal with cases more efficiently.
Designed around our customers
Teams from across DVLA have developed this service, including colleagues who deal with drivers' medical applications every day.

We've reviewed and updated our medical questionnaires, tested the journeys with customers who have a range of conditions, and designed the service to ask the right questions based on the information they provide.
Importantly, we've built the service so we can continue improving it. As customer needs change, we can update questions and journeys more easily without having to redesign the whole service.
We'll continue looking at how we can make the service simpler and enable even more people to deal with us online.
Check if you need to tell DVLA
Having a health condition does not necessarily mean you need to stop driving, and not every condition needs to be reported to us. The easiest way to check is on GOV.UK.
The online service is currently only available for Group 1 drivers (car and motorcycle licence holders).
If you do need to tell us, the online service will guide you through what you need to do, making it as straightforward as possible to give us the information we need.

description: Natalie Morgan, Service Designer at DVLA, explains how we’re making it easier for drivers to tell us about a health condition online, and looks at the latest improvements that mean even more customers can now use the service.

title: Modernising air quality information for the public

content.content: Air quality affects all of us, yet it is often something we cannot see. For people living with asthma, heart disease and other health conditions, poor air quality can have a significant impact on daily life. That's why the Air Quality and Industrial Emissions team have been working on the Check air quality service – to help make trusted air quality information easier to find, understand and act upon.
Why we needed the service

This service is part of Defra’s work to improve public understanding of air pollution. It follows the government’s response to the death of 9-year-old Ella Adoo-Kissi-Debrah, the first person in the world to have air pollution recorded as a cause of death.

Air quality affects everyone, but it can be difficult to understand. Most people do not spend their time thinking about air pollution forecasts, monitoring stations or pollutant measurements. What they want to know is simple: what is air quality like where I am, what does it mean for me, and do I need to do anything differently today?
This challenge sits at the heart of the project.
Putting users at the centre

As a content designer, my job is to make complex information simple, accessible and useful. Air quality is a particularly challenging topic because it combines science, health advice, environmental policy and technical data. We need to explain concepts like pollution forecasts, monitoring networks and health guidance in a way that people can understand quickly, especially when they are making decisions about their day.

From the beginning, the project has focused on understanding user needs. Research shows that people want information that's relevant to where they live, work or spend time. They want reliable data from a trusted source, clear explanations of what pollution levels mean and practical advice they can act on.
Iterate, test, discuss, repeat

We regularly test the service with the public to understand what works and what doesn't. Feedback consistently shows the importance of keeping information simple, reducing clutter and making the important stuff easy to find.

One of the most rewarding parts of the project has been developing the air pollution alerts. Users can select locations that matter to them, such as their home, workplace or local park, and receive alerts by text message or email when high levels of air pollution are forecast. This transforms air quality information from something people must search for into a service that proactively supports informed decision-making.
For citizens, the outcome is simple: trusted information, available in one place, when and where they need it.
Supporting Defra's wider goals
The Check air quality service is about much more than publishing information online.
It supports Defra's wider goal of improving the environment while helping people make informed decisions about their health and wellbeing.

Alongside the Get air pollution data service, it also helps Defra be more transparent - by making government-held air quality information easier to access and understand. I’ll blog about this work soon.
What I've learned
This project is reinforcing something I have always believed about content design: good public services are not created by publishing more information.
They're created by understanding what people need and presenting the right information at the right time in a way that helps them achieve their goal.

The best feedback I heard during research wasn't about air quality science or technical features. It was when someone told us the service was "easy to use – does what it says on the tin". This has been a useful reminder throughout the project and influences many of the decisions we make.

The Check air quality service continues to evolve, and there's plenty more to do. But I'm proud of the role my team have played in helping make important public information more accessible, understandable and useful.
If you've used the service, I'd love to hear about your experience. What helped? What could be improved? Sharing your feedback helps us continue to build services that work for everyone.
More information

title: Your guide to flu vaccination this winter

content.content: Getting your flu vaccine is a practical step towards staying well.
It helps reduce your risk of serious illness and hospital treatment.
Vaccinating children helps protect them and also helps reduce the spread of flu to families and people who are more vulnerable.
Booking arrangements and eligibility can differ elsewhere in the UK.
Why getting vaccinated matters

Flu usually comes on quickly, with fever, aches, exhaustion and a cough. It can cause pneumonia and worsen existing conditions. Even children without a long-term condition sometimes need hospital care. UKHSA estimates that vaccination prevented around 100,000 hospitalisations and 7,000 deaths in England in 2025/26. These are modelled estimates, not a guarantee of individual protection. Protection wanes and flu viruses change, so a vaccine is needed each season.
Who can get a free NHS flu vaccine?

Conditions that can qualify include diabetes, certain breathing conditions such as asthma requiring steroid treatment and COPD, heart disease, chronic kidney or liver disease, some neurological conditions, a learning disability, weakened immunity, spleen problems and a body mass index of 40 or above. Not every long-term condition automatically qualifies: ask your GP, specialist or pharmacist if you are unsure.
How and when to get vaccinated:

Vaccination started on 1 September for pregnant women and eligible children, and on 1 October for most other eligible groups. Participating pharmacies can vaccinate two- and three-year-olds and, since 1 October, children aged two to 17 in clinical risk groups.

Pharmacy catch-up for school-aged children who missed the school offer starts on 1 December 2026, not before. Get vaccinated as soon as you can: protection takes around two weeks to develop. Eligible adults can still receive vaccination later in winter; the NHS adult page lists 31 March 2027 as the final vaccination date.
Stay warm and get help early

Cold weather can worsen heart and lung conditions and increase health risks, particularly for older people and those with existing conditions. Vaccination protects against flu; it does not protect against every effect of cold weather. UKHSA advises trying to heat frequently used rooms, such as your living room and bedroom, to at least 18°C, wearing layers and checking on people who may need support. If heating costs are a problem, ask your council or an advice service about available help. Seek medical advice early if you feel unwell or are worried about someone else.
How the NHS is preparing for winter

The government’s 18 October announcement set out almost £140 million for 14 new urgent care schemes across England, including urgent treatment centres, same day emergency care services, new ambulance fleets and emergency department upgrades. Separately, 25 new or expanded urgent care sites announced in April will be open for winter. These are planned investments and openings, not a claim that every scheme is already operating.

The NHS has been preparing since July following a summer of record activity and extreme heat. The announcement also sets out almost £2 billion in urgent care capital investment until 2030, alongside £1.5 billion already confirmed for urgent maintenance across NHS buildings and facilities. The immediate £140 million announcement should not be added to these wider totals as though each were a separate pot. Extra capacity and vaccination work together: services prepare to treat people who need care, while vaccination helps prevent serious flu illness and avoidable admissions. You should still seek urgent or emergency help when you need it.
Additional questions and practical support

I had a flu vaccine last year. Do I need another?Yes. Protection decreases over time and the vaccine is updated to match the main circulating flu viruses which change over time. If you are eligible, get vaccinated every season.

Can the vaccine give me flu?The injected vaccine cannot cause flu. The children’s nasal spray contains weakened viruses and is designed not to cause flu in eligible children. A runny nose, mild fever or aches after vaccination are not the same as catching flu. The vaccinator checks whether the nasal spray is suitable.

What side effects might I have?Common effects include soreness where an injection was given, mild aches or a slightly raised temperature. Children receiving the nasal spray may have a runny or blocked nose. Effects are usually mild and short-lived. Serious allergic reactions are rare; tell the vaccinator about any previous severe vaccine reaction or allergy and seek medical help if you are concerned.

Is flu vaccination recommended during pregnancy?Yes, at any stage. Flu can be more serious during pregnancy, and vaccination helps protect you and your baby. Ask your midwife, GP or pharmacist about getting vaccinated. Pregnancy eligibility for flu does not automatically mean eligibility for COVID-19 vaccination.

My child missed vaccination at school. What should I do?Contact the school immunisation team about another session. From 1 December 2026, participating pharmacies will also offer school-age catch-up. Children aged two to 17 with clinical risk conditions can already use participating pharmacies; eligible babies under two receive an injected vaccine through their GP. The nasal spray is not routinely offered to children under two.

What if the nasal spray is unsuitable or I do not want it for my child?Speak to the school immunisation team or GP. An injected alternative is available for eligible children when the spray is unsuitable, including when its porcine gelatine content is a concern. Tell the team about asthma, wheezing, weakened immunity, medicines and allergies so they can advise on the right vaccine.

I feel well and manage my condition. Is vaccination still important?Yes, if your condition makes you eligible. Feeling well does not remove the higher risk of complications from flu. Ask your clinical team if you are unsure whether your condition qualifies.

Can I have flu and COVID-19 vaccines together?Yes, if you are eligible for both and the service offers them together. The eligibility rules are different, so check each vaccine separately. Do not delay your flu vaccination while waiting for another vaccine; ask the vaccinator about arrangements.

Can I be vaccinated if I have a cold or have already had flu?A minor illness without a high temperature does not usually prevent vaccination. If you have a high temperature, wait until you are better and ask your provider about rearranging. Even after flu, vaccination can help protect against other strains covered by the vaccine.

Will vaccination stop every flu infection?No vaccine provides complete protection. Flu vaccination reduces the risk of infection and serious illness, but you may still catch flu or another respiratory virus. Continue to wash your hands, cover coughs and sneezes, and avoid close contact with others if you are unwell with a high temperature or cannot do your normal activities.

I cannot book online, need an interpreter or need help attending. What support is available?Call 119 free of charge and ask for an interpreter if needed. Textphone users can use 18001 119; a British Sign Language interpreter service is available through NHS 119. NHS England provides translated, audio, BSL and easy-read vaccination information. Ask the provider in advance for reasonable adjustments, such as a quieter appointment or support from a carer. If you cannot leave home, contact your GP about local home-visit arrangements.

I do not have a fixed address or GP registration. Can I still get help?Yes. Eligible people can get a free flu vaccine at a participating walk-in pharmacy without GP registration. Online national booking requires registration with a GP in England. You do not need proof of address to register with a GP; ask a hostel, day centre, outreach team or local practice for support. People aged 16 or over sleeping rough or using homeless hostels or night shelters are eligible under the new offer.

What if I am not eligible for a free vaccine?Some pharmacies and employers offer vaccination privately. Check availability and costs directly. If you think the eligibility check is wrong, speak to your GP or pharmacist rather than assuming you cannot be vaccinated.

Where should I seek help if I get flu?Ask for an urgent GP appointment or contact NHS 111 if you have flu symptoms and are in a higher-risk group, feel very unwell, are short of breath, are worried about your child or do not improve after seven days. Call 999 or go to A&E for sudden chest pain, severe difficulty breathing or coughing up blood. Do not let concerns about winter pressure delay emergency care.

Why get vaccinated if the NHS is adding more urgent care capacity?Extra services help the NHS care for people who become ill, but preventing serious illness remains important. Almost £140 million has been announced for 14 urgent care schemes, with a separate 25 new or expanded sites opening for winter. Your flu vaccine helps reduce your risk of serious illness and hospital treatment. Getting vaccinated supports these preparations, but it does not replace medical care if you become unwell.

title: Three days of admin down to 10 minutes: the payment switch freeing up school finance teams
authors: Louise Green, DfE Senior Communication and Content Manager

content.content: Reviewing banking arrangements is one of the practical steps schools and trusts can take to ensure every pound is managed as efficiently as possible and directed towards children's education.
Here is what Our Lady of Lourdes Catholic Multi-Academy Trust gained by switching from petty cash to payment cards:
Read on to find out how they did it and what it could mean for your school.
A manual process that was not keeping up

Our Lady of Lourdes Catholic Multi-Academy Trust runs 36 schools across Lincolnshire and Nottinghamshire, with around 13,200 students and an annual budget of £99 million. Managing everyday purchases across schools spread over a wide area was a significant administrative burden.

When the Trust was formed and all financial processing moved to a centralised team, managing petty cash across so many sites was quickly identified as impractical. The decision was made to move to Multipay corporate payment cards instead, giving the finance team far greater control over day-to-day spending.

However, the early setup still had its challenges. Each card had its own individual account and monthly statement. Cardholders had to complete a manual return each month, statements had to be downloaded one by one from the bank’s portal, and the two then reconciled by hand. The resulting data was then keyed manually into the finance system. Every month, that added up to around three full working days.

Management Accountant Paul Kiernan says the old system was holding the team back. "It was a very clunky system that could easily get backed up. What used to take three days of processing every month has now become a 10-minute job, making life an awful lot easier and less stressful."
The first fix: swapping paper for payment cards
The Trust replaced petty cash with corporate payment cards. Headteachers and office managers each received a card, with additional cards issued to other staff based on school size and need.

The key difference was control. The finance team can set spending limits, restrict where cards can be used, and adjust those rules quickly through an online platform - no lengthy approval process required. For day-to-day purchases like breakfast club supplies or classroom materials, cards work where invoicing is not an option. For larger items like school trips, limits can be raised as needed.
All spending is visible in one place - what was spent, where, and by whom. VAT-compliant reporting is automated, reducing the risk of errors and simplifying audits.
The next step: automating the reconciliation process

The real transformation came when their bank introduced the Market Data Collection (MDC) tool. MDC is a web-based platform that collects transaction data for reporting and financial analysis. Rather than downloading individual statements and reconciling them by hand, transactions are now logged directly on the portal. Cardholders receive an automatic email prompt to review their transactions, input the relevant financial coding, and upload a copy of their receipt — all in one place.

The information is then available to the Trust's finance team in a format that maps directly to their finance system. After the required checks, the data can be bulk uploaded to the accounts, replacing what was once hours of manual data entry with a process that takes minutes.
Small changes, big difference
The gains did not come from a large team or a big budget. They came from replacing slow, manual processes with ones that are fast, visible, and easy to control.
If your school or trust is still managing petty cash or paper expense forms, this is worth a closer look.
Speak to your bank today to find out how quickly your school or trust could make the switch.
Further support from the Department for Education
For more tools and guidance on managing your school or trust's finances effectively, visit the schools financial benchmarking and efficiency tools on GOV.UK.
You can also find more blogs on getting the most from your budget on the Buying for Schools blog.

title: No limits: the people living with health conditions and disabilities shaping our justice system
authors: Melissa OGorman, Senior External Communications and Engagement Manager

content.content: [English] - [Cymraeg]

Behind every judgment delivered, every case managed, and every hearing held, there is a person — judges, lawyers, court staff and judicial office holders who bring their own experiences and perspectives to the work they do.

For many colleagues across the justice system, that includes living with a medical condition, disability or long-term health challenge - experiences that often become a source of strength rather than a limitation.

This autumn, the Royal Courts of Justice will welcome Justice Without Limits, an exhibition celebrating the experiences, strengths and contributions of people who live with a medical condition, or are disabled, and who work across the justice sector. Officially launched on Tuesday 27 October, the exhibition showcases photography and personal stories from HMCTS colleagues, members of the judiciary and legal professionals.

The exhibition features a diverse range of roles and conditions, from courtroom staff to judicial office holders, each sharing their story in their own words. Here, we're pleased to share two of those stories.
Lauren, Senior Operations Manager, HMCTS

In 2015, while studying Criminology and Social Policy, I was diagnosed with Systemic Lupus Erythematosus, a chronic autoimmune condition that causes fatigue, joint pain, and a weakened immune system. After graduating, I pursued my dream of joining the Metropolitan Police, successfully passed every aptitude and fitness test. However, the medical assessment brought that ambition to an unexpected end.

A friend suggested looking at opportunities in the Civil Service, and I joined as a Judge's Clerk. Nearly a decade later, I manage two county courts, one being the largest county court in England and Wales. I take pride in building supportive teams and delivering reliable services to court users.

My lupus is now stable, but I continue to manage chronic fatigue, joint pain, and vulnerability to serious illness. In 2024, I was hospitalised with meningitis. As an invisible condition, most of my colleagues are unaware that I live with lupus, but that invisibility has shaped me in many ways. I've championed reasonable adjustments, helping managers support their teams with confidence.

I also sit as a Magistrate in criminal cases, which feels like a full-circle moment and a connection to my original ambitions. Living with an invisible illness has taught me to never judge a book by its cover, a mindset that is invaluable both in the courtroom and as a leader.
Simon, Disability Qualified Panel Member, Social Security and Child Support Tribunal

I lost my leg above the knee in my twenties while studying law. The amputation initially created a mental block about continuing that path, so my experience led me into a career as a prosthetist instead, a vocation directly shaped by what I'd been through. My complex rehabilitation involved several complications that took time to work through.

Becoming a Judicial Office Holder reconnected me with an ambition I thought was closed to me. As a Disability Qualified Panel Member, I sit with a judge and medical colleague hearing benefits appeals. Many appellants are vulnerable, so ensuring hearings are accessible, respectful, and that people feel genuinely heard is crucial to everything I do.

My role translates clinical evidence into real-world impact, focusing on what appellants can reliably and safely do in daily life, not just diagnoses or paperwork. Living with limb loss gives me practical understanding of how disability affects functioning in ways medical records simply don't capture. I know disability can be visible or hidden, that people present differently depending on context, and that reality is often more complex than it appears. I also experience ongoing musculoskeletal and mental health challenges from my amputation, which inform my empathy in every hearing.
A system shaped by lived experience

Lauren and Simon's stories reflect something integral to Justice Without Limits: that the experiences people bring with them, including the challenges they've faced, often become a source of strength in their professional lives. Whether that's Lauren's determination to build supportive teams, or Simon's unique insight into how disability affects day-to-day life beyond what paperwork can show, these perspectives make our justice system stronger and more representative of the society it serves.
Find out more
The exhibition will be on display at the Royal Courts of Justice until Christmas, with a virtual version also available online to ensure it can be experienced by those unable to visit in person.

Mae fy lupus bellach yn sefydlog, ond rwy'n parhau i reoli blinder cronig, poen cymalau, a bregusrwydd i salwch difrifol.  Yn 2024, cefais fy anfon i'r ysbyty gyda llid yr ymennydd.  Fel cyflwr anweledig, nid yw'r rhan fwyaf o fy nghydweithwyr yn ymwybodol fy mod yn byw gyda lupus, ond mae'r anweledigrwydd hwnnw wedi fy siapio mewn sawl ffordd.  Rwyf wedi hyrwyddo addasiadau rhesymol, gan helpu rheolwyr i gefnogi eu timau yn hyderus.

Rwyf hefyd yn eistedd fel Ynad mewn achosion troseddol, daeth hynny â mi drwy gylch llawn a chysylltiad â'm huchelgeisiau gwreiddiol.  Mae byw gyda salwch anweledig wedi fy nysgu i beidio byth â barnu llyfr yn ôl ei glawr, meddylfryd sy'n amhrisiadwy yn y llys ac fel arweinydd.
Simon, Aelod Anabl Cymwysedig o'r Panel, y Tribiwnlys Nawdd Cymdeithasol a Chynnal Plant

Collais fy nghoes uwchben y pen-glin yn fy ugeiniau wrth astudio'r gyfraith.  I ddechrau, creodd y ffaith fy mod i wedi gorfod torri'r goes i ffwrdd rwystr meddyliol ynglŷn â pharhau â'r llwybr hwnnw, felly arweiniodd fy mhrofiad fi i yrfa fel prosthetydd yn lle hynny, galwedigaeth wedi'i siapio'n uniongyrchol gan yr hyn roeddwn i wedi bod drwyddo.  Roedd fy ngwaith adsefydlu cymhleth yn cynnwys sawl cymhlethdod a gymerodd amser i weithio drwyddo.

Mae dod yn Ddeilydd Swydd Farnwrol yn fy ailgysylltu ag uchelgais yr oeddwn i'n meddwl ei fod ar gau i mi.  Fel Aelod Anabl Cymwysedig o'r Panel, rwy'n eistedd gyda barnwr a chydweithiwr meddygol yn gwrando ar apeliadau budd-daliadau.  Mae llawer o apelwyr yn agored i niwed, felly mae sicrhau bod gwrandawiadau yn hygyrch, yn barchus, a bod pobl yn teimlo eu bod yn cael eu clywed wirioneddol yn hanfodol i bopeth rwy'n ei wneud.

Mae fy rôl yn cyfleu tystiolaeth glinigol i effaith yn y byd go iawn, gan ganolbwyntio ar yr hyn y gall apelwyr ei wneud yn ddibynadwy ac yn ddiogel mewn bywyd bob dydd, nid dim ond diagnosisau neu waith papur.  Mae byw gyda cholli aelodau yn rhoi dealltwriaeth ymarferol i mi o sut mae anabledd yn effeithio ar weithredu mewn ffyrdd nad yw cofnodion meddygol yn eu cipio.  Rwy'n gwybod y gall anabledd fod yn weladwy neu gudd, bod pobl yn cyflwyno'n wahanol yn dibynnu ar gyd-destun, a bod realiti yn aml yn fwy cymhleth nag y mae'n ymddangos.  Rwyf hefyd yn profi heriau cyhyrysgerbydol ac iechyd meddwl parhaus ers torri fy nghoes i ffwrdd, sy'n llywio fy empathi ym mhob gwrandawiad.
System wedi'i siapio gan brofiad go iawn

Mae straeon Lauren a Simon yn adlewyrchu rhywbeth sy'n rhan annatod o Justice Without Limits: bod y profiadau y mae pobl yn dod â nhw, gan gynnwys yr heriau maen nhw wedi'u hwynebu, yn aml yn dod yn ffynhonnell cryfder yn eu bywydau proffesiynol.  P'un a yw hynny'n benderfyniad Lauren i adeiladu timau cefnogol, neu fewnwelediad unigryw Simon i sut mae anabledd yn effeithio ar fywyd bob dydd y tu hwnt i'r hyn y gall gwaith papur ei ddangos, mae'r safbwyntiau hyn yn gwneud ein system gyfiawnder yn gryfach ac yn fwy cynrychioliadol o'r gymdeithas y mae'n ei gwasanaethu.

title: Renewing the Technology Code of Practice to support better technology decisions
authors: Ben Hannan, Service owner for Enterprise Architecture, GDS

content.content: Renewing the Technology Code of Practice

The Technology Code of Practice is a set of criteria to help government design, build and buy technology. It has supported public sector teams to make technology decisions since 2013, but it has not evolved with the changing landscape of modern technology and delivery.

The blueprint for modern digital government also sets out a requirement for a “radical consolidation of guidance and standards for digital and technology, retiring out-of-date and duplicative things, updating critical ones, streamlining the information teams need and making it easier for them to understand what to do”.
As such, we are renewing the Code so that it remains practical, relevant and easier to apply, and we want practitioners to help shape what comes next.
What we've heard so far

As part of the review, we've been carrying out user research with colleagues in digital and data professions across the public sector to understand how the Technology Code of Practice is being used today and where it could better support organisations from both a local and national perspective, delivering technology-enabled services.

While the principles remain widely recognised and valued, we've heard that users want guidance that is easier to navigate and clearer about what's expected. We've also heard a desire for guidance that evolves alongside changes in areas such as architecture, cyber security and artificial intelligence.
Those conversations have helped us identify where we can make the biggest improvements first.
Taking the first steps
Our initial focus has been on improving the content and making the purpose of each part of the Code clearer.

We’ve refreshed the homepage to give greater prominence to the principles and introduced a more consistent layout within the sections for user needs, technology architecture and lifecycle management. These areas were chosen because they provide important foundations for organisations making technology decisions and planning for long-term success.

The purpose of the Technology Code of Practice, as well as distinctions between requirements and recommendations have also been clarified to help make it clearer to users when and how to apply it. We’ve also begun removing content that no longer sits within scope of modern technology delivery to make it easier to see only what’s relevant.
Together, these changes represent the first step in helping public sector colleagues make better, more informed technology decisions.
Looking ahead
We're taking an iterative approach to renewal.

For future updates, we’d like to focus on responding to emerging areas of technology, ensuring the standards we publish remain practical in line with the evolving ways government designs, buys and operates technology.  We will also explore options for improving discoverability and navigation changes, alongside continuing improvements to the existing content.
Help us shape what comes next

The insight we've gathered so far has come directly from people across the public sector, and we will continue to reach out as co-design will remain central to how we develop the standards we publish.
