title: Valuing and investing in biodiversity internationally for national security at home

content.content: Earlier this week Defra’s Minister for Nature, Jenny Riddell-Carpenter, announced £28 million of funding to help support countries in the global south to develop their economies without harming biodiversity, and to invest in their own natural capital.
And today at COP17, Minister Riddell-Carpenter hosted an event discussing how to move beyond the conceptual case for nature security, to showcase implementation in practice.
Biodiversity is worth protecting in and of itself. For the countless plant and animal species we share our planet with, and the intrinsic wonder and beauty they give us. That value is incalculable.
But biodiversity and key ecosystems around the world also underpin our economies, our food and water security, supply chains and, we now know, our national security.

In January we published our national security assessment on global biodiversity loss and ecosystem collapse. Its message was clear: ecosystem degradation is not only an environmental challenge, but a strategic risk to UK security and prosperity. As natural systems degrade, risks can cascade across food and water security, economic resilience, supply chains and geopolitical stability.

Therefore, biodiversity does have a value. And that value is felt all around us: in the water we drink, the food we eat, the resilience of our communities, and through our economic resilience and national security.

Yet it rarely appears on balance sheets, or in investment decisions. We need to make the invisible, visible; bringing nature's value into the evidence and policies that shape finance, investment and growth. Doing that demands action.

And so, part of the funding announced this week will go to support the work of the United Nations Development Programme's (UNDP) Biodiversity Finance Initiative (Biofin) and to Financial Sector Deepening Africa’s (FSD Africa) Nature Programme.

These initiatives help countries put biodiversity at the heart of economic and financial decision-making, through identifying and reforming environmentally harmful subsidies, making public spending more effective, mobilising private finance for biodiversity and putting it at the heart of board room’s decision-making.
Much of this work will take place in countries hosting these critical ecosystems, while supporting our commitments on delivery of the Global Biodiversity Framework Targets 14, 15, 18 and 19.
Protecting biodiversity is not simply an environmental objective. It is an investment in our economic resilience and our national security.
Aligning public budgets and private capital with nature
Below Onno from Biofin and Dorothy from FSD Africa talk about how their work develops resilient economies by including nature in economic decisions and attracting public and private investment.
Onno van den Heuvel, Global Lead for Nature Finance at UNDP, said:
"Redesigning subsidies that harm nature presents an immense opportunity to close the finance gap, especially in an era of strained public budgets and declining Official Development Assistance.

"According to an estimate by the Paulson Institute, globally “governments spend more subsidising nature’s destruction in one month than they do on biodiversity protection in an entire year.” The UK’s support to Biofin will enable governments in 138 countries to screen and redesign subsidies that contribute to nature loss.

"In Thailand, Ecuador and Colombia, this work has already demonstrated impact at scale, with millions of dollars in savings to public budgets and a greening of agricultural credit that delivers co-benefits for the climate, livelihoods and gender equality.
"The idea that countries must choose between economic growth and protecting nature is fundamentally flawed.

"A transition to a nature-positive economy could unlock US$10.1 trillion in annual business value and create 395 million jobs by 2030, through changes in how we produce food, build infrastructure and meet our energy needs. The support to Biofin will drive that systemic transformation by de-risking and incentivising investments that can deliver nature-positive economic growth."
Dororthy Maseke, Nature Finance Lead at FSD Africa, said:

"Crucial to this transformation is changing how the financial sector builds nature into policy and investment decisions. Institutions that understand their dependence on nature can better value, invest in, and protect it.

"Nowhere is this more important than Africa, where up to 62% of GDP is highly or moderately dependent on nature. Investing in nature is not only about protecting habitats such as the Congo Basin, the world’s second largest rainforest and a critical carbon sink. It is about livelihoods and economic stability.

"The World Bank estimates the Congo Basin’s forests provided ecosystem services worth US$1.15 trillion in 2020, over 90% of it from global climate regulation. Yet shifting agriculture, urban expansion and land pressures saw the forest cover reduced by 8.6 million hectares (equivalent to over a third of the total size of the United Kingdom) between 2000 and 2020.
"Today’s support for FSD Africa and the African Natural Capital Alliance will help influence investment decisions and mobilise private finance to protect and restore this landscape.

"FSD Africa will work with Central African regulators, banks and insurers to apply the Taskforce on Nature-related Financial Disclosures for identifying, assessing and disclosing nature-related risks and opportunities and develop a regional roadmap for adopting it.

"Through ANCA, the continent’s leading platform for nature-positive finance, we will connect institutions to share learning and help build a pipeline of high-integrity investments that draws private capital into the region’s natural assets."

description: Our fifth COP17 blog post explains why international support for nature has benefits at home as well as abroad.

title: New vape and nicotine rules explained

content.content: New rules on selling and promoting vaping and nicotine products take effect across the UK on 29 October 2026.

They extend protections for under-18s, restrict promotional giveaways and substantial discounts, ban most vending-machine sales and give enforcement authorities additional fixed penalty powers. Here is what is changing, why we are making these changes and what happens if the law is not followed.
Why are we making these changes?

We want to protect children from nicotine addiction while maintaining vaping as a quit aid for adult smokers. The changes close gaps in age-of-sale rules, prevent adults from buying products on behalf of children and restrict promotions that encourage uptake.

Marketing and promotion are factors behind youth vaping. Stronger enforcement powers help authorities act against breaches and support retailers who follow the law. This is part of the phased implementation of the Tobacco and Vapes Act and supports the 10 Year Health Plan for England’s shift from sickness to prevention.
Which products cannot be sold to under-18s?

From 29 October, it is illegal to sell any vaping product or non-medicinal nicotine product to someone under 18, whether online or in a shop. This covers vape devices, e-liquids with or without nicotine, related components such as coils and pods, and nicotine pouches, strips and pearls. Products containing synthetic nicotine are also covered. Medicinally licensed products are subject to separate medicines legislation.

Selling nicotine-containing vapes to under-18s was already illegal. England, Wales and Northern Ireland are extending their rules to nicotine-free vaping products; Scotland already restricted their sale to under-18s. The changes also bring other nicotine products, such as tobacco-free nicotine pouches, within the age-of-sale rules. Retailers need to apply age checks to the full range of products covered, not just nicotine-containing vapes.
Can an adult buy a vape or nicotine pouch for a child?

No. Anyone aged 18 or over commits an offence if they buy, or attempt to buy, a vaping or nicotine product on behalf of someone under 18. This is called proxy purchasing. The rule covers nicotine-free vapes and non-medicinal nicotine products as well as nicotine-containing vapes. It prevents an adult purchase being used to get around the age-of-sale restriction.
What is changing for giveaways, discounts and coupons?

Promotional giveaways and substantial promotional discounts are prohibited for vaping and nicotine products, tobacco products, herbal smoking products and cigarette papers. The restrictions also cover giving away coupons, or selling coupons at a substantial discount, for these products. They apply where promotion is the purpose, or where the person knows or has reason to suspect that promotion will be the effect, including in shops and online.

This is not a blanket ban on every price reduction, multibuy or loyalty scheme. Businesses must assess individual offers against the legislation and published guidance: a promotion is not automatically lawful simply because it is described as a discount or clearance sale. Provision by public authorities to support smoking cessation can continue under the Act’s public health defence.
Can these products still be sold from vending machines?

Vending-machine sales of tobacco products, herbal smoking products, cigarette papers, vaping products and nicotine products are prohibited across the UK. The rule also covers machines that dispense a product as part of a sale even if the customer pays elsewhere. Responsibility rests with the person who has management or control of the premises where the machine is available for customer use.

A limited exemption allows vending machines selling vaping products in adult inpatient areas of mental health hospitals in England and Wales. It does not extend to nicotine pouches or tobacco products, or to general hospital settings. The wider restriction removes a route through which customers could obtain age-restricted products without a staffed retail sale.
What are the penalties for breaking the rules?

From 29 October, enforcement authorities can issue fixed penalty notices for a range of offences involving these products. In England and Wales, the fixed penalty is £200 for specified offences, with a reduced amount available for prompt payment. A notice gives the recipient an opportunity to avoid prosecution for that offence by paying within the specified period. The notice sets out the payment requirements.

The £200 figure is not a maximum court fine or a penalty that applies to every breach. Enforcement authorities can pursue prosecution, and a court can impose the penalty applicable to the particular offence. Failure to pay a fixed penalty notice can also lead to prosecution for the original offence. The offences covered, fixed penalty amounts and court penalties differ between England, Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland.
Trading Standards lead retail enforcement in England, Wales and Scotland, with district councils responsible in Northern Ireland.
Does this stop adults using vapes to quit smoking?

No. Legal vaping products remain available to adults. Vaping is less harmful than smoking and can help adult smokers quit, but it is not risk-free. Children and adult non-smokers should never vape. Stop smoking services can continue to support adults, including through product provision covered by the public health defence.
Are these the same as the future tobacco age-of-sale changes?

No. From 1 January 2027, it will be illegal to sell tobacco products, herbal smoking products or cigarette papers to anyone born on or after 1 January 2009. Anyone born after this date will never be legally sold tobacco. That is separate from the vaping and nicotine age-of-sale rules taking effect on 29 October – where the age of sale is 18.
The intended comprehensive advertising and sponsorship ban from 1 June 2027, and future decisions on packaging, flavours, displays and smoke-free or vape-free places, are also separate measures.
What is a substantial discount?

A substantial discount is a price reduction that significantly lowers the cost of a product compared with its standard selling price. Whether a discount is substantial can vary depending on the product and the type of promotion. Selling products or coupons at a substantial discount is being banned to stop businesses trying to find a way round the free distribution offence.

Selling e-liquid, vape devices or nicotine products to customers in-store or through online promotions at a nominal sum, such as 10p, would likely be an offence. The substantial discount offence also applies to products that have the purpose or effect of promoting a vaping or nicotine product without being one of these products.

For example, a vape charger with vaping product branding. These restrictions do not affect normal discounting practices. Retailers can continue to sell unsold stock at a reduced price as part of normal business. Bulk and trade discounts may still apply.
Where can I find the guidance for these changes?
Guidance for all of the changes coming in on 29 October and 1 January can be found on GOV.UK: Smoking and vaping: guidance, policy and regulation - GOV.UK

title: Tracking funding for nature: the 2026 Biodiversity Finance Trends Dashboard

content.content: Protecting nature costs money, and the world is still falling well short of what's needed.
The 2026 Biodiversity Finance Trends Dashboard was launched at the start of the 17th UN Biodiversity Conference.

Produced by the UK government and The Nature Conservancy, the dashboard tracks how much finance is flowing towards protecting nature, and how much there is still to go. It shows where things are moving in the right direction, and where the gaps are.

To halt and reverse biodiversity loss by 2030 will require at least $200 billion for nature. Plus, at least $500 billion a year that is currently spent on incentives that harm nature needs to be reduced or redirected.
International finance is rising, and businesses are taking notice of nature
The Dashboard shows that finance flowing from developed to developing countries to protect nature has more than doubled since 2019, to almost $19 billion in 2024.

It’s good progress, but it's a stepping stone: by 2030, international finance needs to reach $30 billion a year, as part of the wider $200 billion a year from all sources. Keeping up this pace of growth is essential.

Businesses are also taking nature risk more seriously. More than 800 organisations across 50-plus countries, managing $26.2 trillion in assets, have now committed to reporting on how their businesses depend on nature, and how their businesses impact nature.
This matters because it helps organisations understand their risks and responsibilities when it comes to looking after nature which they rely upon.

Private money is starting to flow too. The Dashboard showcases the Cali Fund which allows businesses to put direct finance back into nature. It allows companies that profit from genetic data from nature to contribute and to protect it, with at least half of that money set aside to support indigenous peoples and local communities.
So far, five businesses have contributed or committed to contribute. It's early days, but it's a promising route for private finance to flow towards and support nature.
Progress on cutting funding that harms nature is slow but steady
Countries have committed to reducing subsidies and incentives that harm nature by at least $500 billion a year by 2030 – and there are positive signs that action is being taken.

105 countries now have nature-friendly incentives in place, and 39 have completed full reviews of their harmful subsidies using the United Nations Development Programme Biodiversity Finance Initiative guidance, with many more underway or planned.
However, spotting harmful incentives is just the first step. Countries now need to reduce or redirect these incentives fairly, and in a way that supports people through the change.
Getting money where it's needed, and countries building their own plans
Global funding targets only matter if the finance raised reaches the people and places that can use it.
The Global Biodiversity Framework Fund has so far allocated $362 million to 82 projects in 87 countries, including many small island and least developed nations.

In the Solomon Islands, the fund has empowered local communities to protect 20,000 hectares of critical ecosystems by creating a community-led trust fund and promoting sustainable, women-led businesses.
Many countries are also developing their own national plans for financing nature protection: 41 have completed these, and 136 more have started.
Meanwhile, 19 countries and regions are developing or exploring biodiversity credit schemes, an emerging approach that will need strong rules to ensure it works as intended.
What this all means

This year's Dashboard shows real signs of progress: more international funding, more businesses reporting on nature risk, closer scrutiny of harmful subsidies, and more countries building their own plans.

But the $700 billion gap will not close through any one source of funding alone. Governments, businesses, investors and development organisations all have a part to play, both in raising new money and in redirecting funding that currently works against nature.
Clear, accurate data like this helps everyone see what's working, where the gaps are, and where more international co-operation is needed, as countries move from promises to action.
Read the full 2026 Biodiversity Finance Trends Dashboard and technical annex.

title: Showing up together: why good health starts long before you reach a hospital

content.content: By Oliver Harmar, Natural England's Chief Strategy Officer

Leaders from national bodies including Natural England, Sport England and NHS England met at the Cabinet Office to explore how to work together to support healthier places. Oliver Harmer reflects on the 20-year gap in healthy life expectancy, a joined-up approach being tested in the West Midlands, and why good health is created in the "gloriously ordinary" parts of everyday life.
Earlier this month, I had the privilege of chairing a meeting hosted by the Cabinet Office that felt different from most I attend in government.

Around the table were leaders from across government: Natural England, Active Travel England, Sport England, Arts Council England, Historic England, NHS England, Homes England, West Midlands Combined Authority, and the Cabinet Office's Test, Learn and Grow team.

The question we had come together to answer was simple to ask, but hard to answer: how do we better align nationally, so we can show up together and support local leaders to create the conditions for good health?

It’s a crucial question, because if you live in one of the least deprived areas of England, you can expect to spend around 20 more years in good health than someone living in one of the most deprived areas. That’s a shocking gap that should motivate us all to act.

We know that health isn't just created in hospitals and GP surgeries. Health outcomes are shaped upstream by factors such as housing, income, transport, physical inactivity and people's wider environment, while the NHS and healthcare often deals with the eventual consequences of ill health. It's created in the parks, libraries, cycle lanes, nature, community choirs, museums, football clubs, the home you live in and the street you walk down.

Each of our organisations already has big ambitions in this space. Natural England helps people access green spaces that lift mental and physical wellbeing, supporting our strategy’s ambition to deliver nature recovery as a foundation for the nation’s growth, health and security. Active Travel England makes it easier and safer for children to walk or cycle to school. Sport England seeks to tackle stubborn inequalities that exist in sport and physical activity by removing the barriers that prevent people, particularly those with the most to gain, from taking part. Arts Council England puts creativity at the heart of healthier communities. Historic England shows how heritage and belonging support happiness and connection.  Homes England creates healthier communities through quality housing and well-designed places.

But here's the challenge we set ourselves: too often we work alongside each other, rather than truly with each other. So, we want to test a new way of working together in the West Midlands to find out what it really looks like when national bodies show up as one team in service of a place.  This will explore questions over joint governance, shared outcome metrics, how to work across organisational boundaries and how activity can connect at national, regional and neighbourhood levels.

We want to be open about what we're learning, including what doesn't work, so other places can learn with us from the start. We know that what works in one place might not be the thing that’s needed in another but hope that we can develop a repeatable model for how ALBs work collectively in places. At its core will be a more joined up approach that listens to place-leaders so that we can all work more effectively together to support healthier households, communities and neighbourhoods across the country.

Ultimately, this is about enabling us all the “gloriously ordinary” things that enrich our lives - a walk in nature, a trip to a local museum, a safe cycle to school, a seat in a community choir.  These everyday activities are where good health is created.

title: Building digital services around business needs
authors: Kieran Housden, Director of OnePlatform, OneLogin for Business programme

content.content: The Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Technology (BIST) is working with the Government Digital Service (GDS) in an exciting collaboration to improve how businesses interact with government online. Director Kieran Housden shares how the programme is developing.

If we’ve heard one thing clearly from businesses so far, it’s that they want government to keep it simple. They want it to be as easy and intuitive as possible, when they need to fill in forms, check regulations or get support to grow.

That’s the driving force behind work to reshape how businesses interact with government online. We’re looking to reduce fragmentation of information between departments and develop a more consistent way for businesses to access government services. This will help reduce duplication and save time.

These are not quick fix things. But we are committed to delivering value as early as we can to businesses and sharing incremental improvements as we go. This summer we made real progress, setting up a new team in the Government Digital Service (GDS) to focus on delivery. You can read our recent blog post to find out more.
Join up for business owners
The programme brings together policy expertise with digital delivery disciplines, putting user needs at the centre of how services for businesses are designed and improved.

We’re working closely with HMRC, Companies House and getting support from colleagues across government who want to share best practice from their service delivery. We are also collaborating with DDaT communities, to test scope and understand what the benefits could be for their customers.
Jess O’Leary is the Deputy Director building the new GDS team, which will focus on our delivery. Jess brings deep experience of developing digital products and services for business.  She says:

For businesses, that will show up as making everyday tasks simpler. It could mean providing the same information fewer times and finding the right support more easily. They could receive more relevant information based on their needs and circumstances or return to a service without having to start again.
Learning and improving as we deliver

Agile working, testing ideas with users early and adjusting as we learn, is key to the development of our solutions. It has been a great learning opportunity for colleagues across the programme. BIST policy and analysis, GDS and BIST Digital, Data and Technology teams are learning from one another’s expertise and experience throughout early research and delivery.

In practice, this means we won't wait until a service is finished before we ask businesses whether it helps them. We're testing early versions with real users, listening to what is and isn't working, and making changes before rolling things out more widely. That should mean services that reflect how businesses operate, and improvements that keep pace as needs change. Success will be measured in practical improvements: fewer repeated steps; clearer and more personalised guidance; and a smoother experience across government services.

As we look towards next year, we’ll begin to improve existing business content online and test new tools, for example for finding funding. It’s the beginning of an exciting journey and we look forward to sharing more as we go.

title: Six months since implementation of the UK’s new clinical trials regulations

content.content: How to avoid delays when submitting clinical trial application assessments

The UK's new clinical trial regulations came into force on 28 April 2026, introducing a more flexible and risk-proportionate approach to clinical trial assessment. Sponsors now submit a single clinical trial application for review by both the MHRA and a Research Ethics Committee (REC) through the Integrated Research Application System (IRAS). The aim is simple: to help potentially life-changing medicines to reach patients faster, while maintaining the highest standards of safety and oversight.
Getting it right first time

The quality and completeness of every application remain essential to making the process work as efficiently as possible. By reviewing the guidance, using the available checklists and providing the right information first time, sponsors can help avoid unnecessary requests for information and support a smoother assessment. In this blog we highlight some common issues encountered by sponsors during assessment and share practical steps you can take to prepare a high-quality application.
Delays to application assessments: Common Issues

title: How waste sites are monitored: who deals with odour and other types of pollution?

content.content: If you live near a waste site, recurring odour pollution or concerns about other types of pollution can quickly become a source of stress.

Monitoring is a shared responsibility. Site operators must monitor and manage their sites. The Environment Agency regulates those sites assesses compliance with permit conditions and acts where necessary to protect people and the environment.
Why environmental monitoring matters

From the Environment Agency’s side, we want to understand whether a waste site is operating as it should, whether permit conditions are being met and whether people or the environment are being affected.
Good environmental monitoring helps identify problems and possible solutions early, informs our regulatory decisions and can also support effective enforcement where necessary.
What is a waste site operator responsible for?
Operators are responsible for monitoring and managing activities at their sites.
The exact requirements vary depending on the type of site and the environmental permit in place.
Monitoring may include:
Operators are required to understand the risks associated with their activities and take effective steps to  prevent pollution and minimise environmental impacts
How does the Environment Agency monitor waste sites?
The Environment Agency independently assesses whether sites are complying with their permit conditions and acts to prevent pollution or where that is not possible, to minimise it.
We do this through a range of activities, including:
We use evidence from multiple sources to build a picture of what is happening at a site.
How is odour pollution monitored and assessed?
Odour pollution is one of the most common concerns raised by communities living near waste management and industrial sites.
Operators may be required to have odour management plans that explain how they will prevent or minimise odour pollution and its impacts.
When we receive reports of odour pollution, our officers investigate to assess whether an odour is present, how strong it is and whether a permitted site is the likely source.
Environment Agency investigations into odour pollution need to account for a wide range of factors.
Weather, wind direction, temperature, other local activities, and their own individual sensitivity can all influence what people experience and where odour travel.
That is one reason why investigations rely on evidence gathered over time rather than assumptions based on a single report.
Why odour pollution reports are important
Reports of odour pollution from a community are a valuable source of information.
They help us identify patterns, understand impacts, the scale of the issue and target to our regulatory activity where it is needed most.
Every odour pollution report adds to the evidence available to us.
However, a confirmed odour pollution report on its own does not automatically mean that permit conditions have been breached.

The Environment Agency has to assess all available information, including monitoring data, site observations, the techniques being used by the operator to control the odour pollution and the evidence gathered by our officers.
How does the Environment Agency investigate waste site pollution reports?
The approach depends on the nature of the concern.
For example, we may:
Our aim is to establish what has happened, whether permit conditions are being met and whether further action is required.
What about other types of pollution?
Odour pollution is only one part of environmental regulation.
Many permits also include conditions designed to manage:
Where concerns are raised, we assess the evidence available and investigate where appropriate.
Different issues may require different forms of monitoring and different regulatory responses.
How we decide what action to take
Not every pollution report will result in immediate enforcement action.
We prioritise our response based on environmental risk and the evidence available.
We consider factors such as:
Where we identify non-compliance, we require operators to  improve their performance rapidly. In more serious cases, we will take formal enforcement action.
What you can do if you are concerned
If you believe a waste site is causing pollution, reporting it helps us build a clearer picture of what communities are experiencing.
The more information you can provide, such as location, timing and the nature of the issue, the more useful it may be in helping us assess the concern.

While we cannot promise a particular outcome from any individual report, community information plays an important role in helping us understand environmental impacts and target our regulatory activity.
Protecting people, places and the environment
People notice when something changes in their local environment.
A persistent odour, unusual or recurring pollution can affect quality of life and confidence in a neighbourhood.
That is why environmental monitoring matters.

By combining operator monitoring, regulatory oversight and information from local communities, we build a picture of risks, focus our efforts where they are most needed and take action to protect people, places and the environment.

You can report pollution to the Environment Agency via our pollution hotline. This is manned 24hrs a day, 365 days a year. The number is 0800 80 70 60.

title: Birds, their supporting habitats and impacts of marine recreation: Understanding the connections
authors: Francesca Della Valle, Marine Conservation Manager

content.content: The English coastline supports a remarkable diversity of bird life. Its rich network of mudflats, saltmarshes and shallow coastal waters provides food and shelter for millions of birds throughout the year.

From gannets plunging into the sea at speeds of up to 60 mph in pursuit of fish, to curlews using their long, curved bills to detect prey hidden beneath mudflats, and avocets sweeping their distinctive upturned beak through shallow water.

Many of these species are protected within Marine Protected Areas (MPAs), including Special Protection Areas (SPAs). This is because they are rare, vulnerable to environmental pressures, or form internationally important breeding, wintering and migratory populations that rely on our coasts and seas for survival.
Impacts of marine recreation

We understand that marine non-licensable activities (mNLA), such as recreational boating, kayaking, paddleboarding, sailing, and wildlife watching trips at sea can sometimes disturb birds, particularly during key periods such as breeding, migration or wintering.
What disturbance looks like

When birds are disturbed, they may stop feeding, become more alert, move away from important habitat or take flight. Although a single disturbance event may seem small, repeated disturbance can reduce the amount of time birds spend feeding and resting. This may increase energy use and, over time, affect survival, breeding success or the ability of birds to build up the energy reserves they need during migration and winter periods.

Disturbance effects from mNLA have been recorded across a wide range of bird groups such as waders, seabirds, and divers. Different groups show different levels of sensitivity, but visual and noise disturbance, such as birds reacting to the presence or sound of nearby vessels, are important factors across all groups.
The marine habitats they depend on

Birds also depend on a wide range of supporting habitats to feed, rest, shelter and breed. Intertidal mudflats and sandflats, for example, are rich feeding grounds where species such as curlews and oystercatchers feed on worms, shellfish and other invertebrates.

Saltmarshes provide places for birds to roost during high tide and can offer shelter from harsh weather. Seagrass beds help support healthy marine ecosystems by providing homes for fish and invertebrates that are an important food source for many bird species. Reefs and rocky habitats support a variety of marine life that attract feeding seabirds, while shallow coastal waters provide important feeding and resting areas for migratory species.

Together, these important habitats help birds build up the energy reserves they need to survive winter, breed successfully and complete long-distance migrations. Given supporting habitats are essential for healthy bird populations, impacts from mNLA to these should also be considered.
Have your say

The MMO is currently seeking additional evidence on the impacts of mNLA on birds, benthic habitats, reef, and seagrass. If you have relevant research, monitoring data, reports or observations, we ask you to respond to our current call for evidence and respond before it closes on 25 November 2026.
By sharing information, you can help improve our understanding of these impacts and support the effective protection of England’s birds and the supporting habitats they rely on.

For more detailed guidance on how to contribute, why this is important and the types of evidence that we find useful, please visit our previous blog: Share your evidence on the impacts of recreational activities in England’s marine protected areas (MPAs) – Marine Development Blog
If you require support completing our survey or submitting evidence, please let us know: conservation@marinemanagement.org.uk

title: Anticipating Exploitation: Using Futures Analysis to Stay Ahead of Modern Slavery Threats

content.content: By Dr Elaine Wedlock, Head of Strategic Analysis, Office of the UK Independent Anti-Slavery Commissioner

Modern slavery is often described as a hidden crime, but one of its greatest challenges is that it is also constantly evolving. The Independent Anti-Slavery Commissioner has a statutory role to encourage good practice in the prevention, detection, investigation and prosecution of modern slavery offences, and in the identification of and support for victims. To fulfil that role effectively, it is essential not only to understand current threats, but also to consider how exploitation may develop in the years ahead.

Through the Government Office for Science's Futures Procurement Framework Co-Funding Initiative, the Independent Anti-Slavery Commissioner’s Office commissioned Decision Analysis Services to undertake a strategic futures analysis examining how modern slavery and human trafficking could change over the next ten years. Exploitation adapts quickly to new conditions. Criminals respond to technological advances, economic pressures, migration patterns and global instability, while policy and operational responses are, understandably, often focused on the challenges of today. The Commissioner recognised the need to create space for longer-term thinking about the risks and trends likely to shape modern slavery and human trafficking without being constrained by policy or operational assumptions.

The result was Anticipating Exploitation: A Futures Analysis. Rather than attempting to predict what will happen, the report is intended to help policymakers, practitioners and partners prepare for a range of plausible futures, strengthening the UK's ability to prevent and respond to evolving forms of exploitation.

The project brought together more than 50 organisations from across government, law enforcement, academia, civil society and survivor-led groups. We also worked closely with people with lived experience of modern slavery and human trafficking, ensuring that futures thinking was grounded in the realities of exploitation today.

Using methods set out in the Government Office for Science Futures Toolkit, the project combined horizon scanning, expert engagement, scenario development and backcasting. Participants identified key drivers that could shape future exploitation and explored how these might interact over the next ten years. The scenarios developed were not forecasts. Instead, they provided a structured way to explore uncertainty, challenge assumptions and test the resilience of current approaches.

One of the most striking findings was not the emergence of entirely new threats, but how many future risks represented an evolution of issues we already see today. Participants repeatedly highlighted the growing role of technology. Artificial intelligence, digital platforms, encrypted communications and cryptocurrencies are creating new opportunities for offenders to recruit, control and profit from victims at greater scale and with greater anonymity. Rather than replacing existing forms of exploitation, technology appears likely to accelerate and amplify them.

We were also struck by the consistency of the messages coming from people with lived experience. During workshops, survivors often identified vulnerabilities and warning signs long before institutions recognised them. In some discussions, participants reflected that issues now being described as emerging risks had been raised by survivors years earlier. This reinforced the importance of embedding lived experience not only in service design and policy development, but also in strategic foresight work.

Another insight was the extent to which modern slavery is connected to wider social, economic and geopolitical trends. Participants highlighted the influence of conflict, climate change, migration pressures, labour market changes and economic instability. The exercise demonstrated that the future of exploitation cannot be understood in isolation from these wider forces, making collaboration across sectors increasingly important.

The project ultimately identified a range of emerging threats, including online-enabled sexual exploitation, gig economy exploitation, visa-related exploitation and the exploitation of vulnerable adults. It also highlighted concerns around the capacity of safeguarding and enforcement systems to keep pace with increasingly adaptive forms of criminality. These findings helped inform a practical action plan focused on prevention, survivor involvement, stronger safeguarding and more effective disruption of offenders.
Looking back, there are several lessons that may be useful for other organisations considering futures projects.

First, diversity of perspectives matters. Some of the richest discussions occurred when policymakers, practitioners, academics and people with lived experience were examining the same scenario from different viewpoints. Bringing those perspectives together helped uncover assumptions and identify blind spots that might otherwise have been missed.

Second, futures work is most valuable when it embraces uncertainty rather than trying to eliminate it. There was a natural temptation to ask which scenario was most likely. However, the real value came from exploring a range of plausible futures and considering what actions would remain beneficial across all of them.

Third, linking foresight to action is critical. The backcasting element of the project helped participants move beyond identifying risks and towards identifying practical interventions. Working backwards from a preferred future created a clear connection between long-term thinking and decisions that can be taken today.

One of the lasting benefits of the project has been demonstrating how futures methods can support responses to complex social harms. Modern slavery and human trafficking are constantly evolving, and organisations need tools that help them navigate uncertainty, not just react to events as they occur. Futures approaches provide a structured way to do this.

Through this work, our priorities and thinking have evolved. We have also been struck by the level of interest it has generated, from small frontline practitioners to our international partners, stimulating discussion and dialogue about the future of modern slavery and the actions needed to prepare for it.

The key message for us is simple. Modern slavery is unlikely to stand still over the coming decade, and neither can our response. Futures work cannot tell us exactly what 2036 will look like. What it can do is help us ask better questions, recognise emerging risks earlier and take action before those risks become entrenched. That has been the greatest value of this project and a reminder that preventing exploitation requires us to anticipate tomorrow's challenges, not just respond to today's.
Report: Anticipating Exploitation: A Futures Based Analysis

The IASC presented this work to the Government Futures Network, a community of futures practitioners and policy makers. If you’re in government and interested in joining the network contact the GO-Science Futures team at futures@go-science.gov.uk.
There are also more case studies about using futures on our website and if you’d like to find out more about commissioning your own futures project take a look here: Futures Procurement Framework.

title: 30by30: How the Natural History Museum turns science into action

content.content: You might be thinking it’s curious for a museum of any kind to have something to say about global biodiversity policy targets. But the Natural History Museum is far more than a beloved visitor attraction and a catalogue of the natural world.

I’m Charlie, and I’m part of the Policy Unit at the Natural History Museum. Over the past few years, we have been combining our scientific expertise with our public reach to help inform effective implementation of 30by30 – a significant global biodiversity target to conserve and manage 30% of land, waters and seas by 2030 – which the UK has committed to.

How do we do this? Our nearly 500 scientists and students work to find nature-based solutions to some of the biggest environmental challenges we face. This includes the researchers who developed the Biodiversity Intactness Index, which is widely recognised as one of the most scientifically robust tools for modelling and understanding local biodiversity around the world.
This is important. If we can’t understand properly what the state of biodiversity worldwide is and, crucially, how it is changing, we can’t know how best to respond.
Making nature protection meaningful
That’s why we are taking this data and applying it to the trickiest environmental challenges that decisionmakers face.

30by30 is one of those challenges. We know the need – some scientists even believe the target should go further – and we have the buy-in to do it. What’s not clear, however, is how best to go about it.
Questions remain over which 30% we should protect, what we should prioritise when considering where to protect, and how to make sure protection is meaningful and not just progress-on-paper.

Our findings on 30by30 are helping to answer some of these outstanding questions. They highlight the importance of protecting the land that delivers the most critical ecosystem services, upon which over six billion people depend for their wellbeing. They also underscore the importance of ensuring that protected areas effectively safeguard biodiversity, which at the moment is declining faster on average across the global protected areas network than outside it.

The impact of these findings reverberates far beyond the walls of conventional environment ministries, with consequences not only for wider national resilience and wellbeing, but also for our ability to meet our climate change targets too.

Our latest analysis also shows that there is no one-size-fits-all solution to achieving 30by30. In fact, how we achieve it and what the world looks like as a result will differ significantly depending on how we value nature, whether prioritising qualities such as endemic species, ecosystem services or cultural landscapes.
From data to action

We are now working hard to take this data out of its spreadsheets and into the hands of delivery partners. We want every community in the UK and internationally to have access to it, empowering everyone to make the best-informed science-backed decisions they can.
For policymakers, this means providing this data and analysis freely and on-demand to anyone around the world, with access to country-level data and maps of biodiversity change.

Already, Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office embassies in regions across the world are using this data and analysis in conversations with partners on the ground to inform local conservation strategies.

For businesses, this means licensing our Biodiversity Intactness Index data to corporates and financial institutions including Bloomberg and BlackRock so that companies can understand their impact on nature and alter their investment and business decisions accordingly.
And for the public, this means sharing this work in a way that galvanises momentum and support for initiatives such as 30by30.
The National Education Nature Park is a Department for Education-sponsored project led by the Natural History Museum in partnership with the Royal Horticultural Society and others.

It is addressing the interconnected challenges of climate change and nature loss by providing a framework for schools, colleges and nurseries in England to enhance young people’s connection with nature and encourage science-backed action for the planet.
The programme is included in Defra’s 30by30 Delivery Plan as an example of how to inspire public participation and buy-in for nature recovery and policy ambition.
Looking forward
As COP17 continues in its second week, we are out in Armenia with our partners to talk about our analysis on 30by30 and our broader work, while connecting with the international community.

This includes working with our partners at the Zoological Society of London and Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew as the UK Biodiversity Alliance, through which we are building optimism by showcasing practical and scalable examples of integrated climate and nature action that are already taking place all around the world.

While the science can be stark, our aim is to share hope. With the right data and the right intentions, meaningful progress for nature can be made. We’ll be advocates for that both at COP17 and beyond.
To find out more about the Natural History Museum’s activities mentioned in this blog, contact Charlie Gold at c.gold@nhm.ac.uk.

title: Strengthening connections between research and regulation

content.content: OPSS reflects on how the 2026 Royal Society Pairing Scheme, supported by the Government Science & Engineering Profession, strengthened connections between research and regulation.
Opening the door to collaboration

When OPSS took part in the Royal Society Pairing Scheme, we hoped it would help us better understand how researchers and regulators can work together to strengthen the evidence that supports effective product regulation. What we gained was a clearer appreciation of the breadth of research taking place across academia that resonates with the work of the Office for Product Safety and Standards (OPSS), together with a better understanding of how regulators can build meaningful connections with external expertise.

We were paired with Dr Rohit Gupta, a Senior Research Fellow at University College London (UCL). A range of teams worked together to plan, deliver and promote the programme. Through work-shadowing activities, laboratory demonstrations, knowledge-sharing and engagement opportunities, colleagues showcased how science and engineering support regulatory decisions.
Inside OPSS and UCL

Rohit participated in work-shadowing activities at OPSS’s London office, engagement with Trade Association stakeholders, visits to our Teddington laboratories, and discussions with colleagues across different functions. He also presented his research to an extended Science Team audience, creating opportunities for exchange between OPSS colleagues and researchers working in areas relevant to future regulatory interests.

The reciprocal visit to UCL was equally valuable. The OPSS Science and Engineering Team visited the Marshgate campus and its Manufacturing Futures Laboratory, the Hawkes Institute and UCL Engineering Buildings. We were warmly welcomed by academics and students who generously shared their work, organised laboratory visits and demonstrations, and discussed both the opportunities and challenges associated with their research. We were impressed by the breadth of expertise across the university and the potential for this research to contribute to future regulatory challenges. The visit also provided an opportunity to explore how academic expertise and facilities could support future evidence needs.
Why engagement matters

A key reflection from the scheme was the value of engaging with academia before specific regulatory questions arise. Building relationships early helps regulators understand where expertise sits, what facilities are available, and how that expertise can be accessed when evidence, testing or scientific advice is needed. For OPSS, the greatest value of the scheme was gaining a clearer understanding of the wider research landscape and strengthening connections that could support future evidence gathering.

The experience also reinforced the importance of helping researchers understand the routes available for engagement with government. We were able to introduce OPSS's scientific engagement activities, including our Areas of Research Interest (ARIs), Registers of Specialists (RoS), the Scientific Advisory Group on Chemical Safety in Consumer Products (SAG-CS), and wider routes for academic engagement.
Continuing the conversation

The pairing has continued to generate interest beyond the exchange. The experience has been shared amongst OPSS colleagues, featured in the OPSS research newsletter, and a LinkedIn post directed readers to a UCL article offering an academic perspective. Together, these activities raise awareness of opportunities for engagement between regulators and the research community.

Most importantly, the scheme demonstrated that meaningful collaboration often begins with conversation. By creating opportunities for researchers and regulators to better understand each other's environments, priorities and challenges, the Royal Society Pairing Scheme helps build relationships that can support evidence gathering and regulatory decision-making. We hope the connections established through this exchange will continue to benefit both OPSS and the wider research community.
If you are an academic and interested in future collaborations, email opss.research@businessandtrade.gov.uk to receive updates about relevant opportunities.

title: What is a Good Level of Development and why does it matter?

content.content: Every year, the government publishes statistics that show how many children have reached a Good Level of Development (GLD) by the end of their Reception year.

Reaching a good level of development is important because it means a child has gained the early skills that will prepare them for starting school and help them thrive later in life. The government has set a target for 75% of all children reaching a GLD by 2028.

The latest figures show that in 2025/26 72.3% of children met the standard, the highest ever level, that's 7 in 10 children having the best start to their education. This means we are well on track to meet the target.
Here's what parents need to know.
How is it measured?

GLD is not an exam or test. Towards the end of Reception, teachers use what they have seen and learnt about a child throughout the year to assess whether they have met specific development goals. These are:
More details on what the goals are can be found here.
Why is it important?
The first five years of a child’s life are crucial. They lay the foundations for what comes next with 90% of a child's brain development taking place before the age of five.

Evidence shows that strong early development supports later learning and increases the likelihood of future success in school and beyond. Getting these foundations right can make a real difference to children's opportunities as they move through school and towards further education, training and work.
That is why the government set an ambition for 75% of five-year-olds to reach a Good Level of Development by 2028 so every child no matter their background or postcode has the best start in life.

What can parents do to help?

There are lots of things you can do at home to support your child’s development. Simple, everyday moments like chatting, playing and reading everyday can make a big difference. You don’t need to have special equipment or take extra time out of your day; there are plenty of fun ways to practice these skills in your daily routine.
Building these habits early can support their development and help them settle into school with confidence. The good news is you are probably doing more than you realise.
For more tips and ideas you can help your child’s development in and around the home, from pregnancy right through to starting school, visit beststartinlife.gov.uk.
Together, this is about helping more children build the skills they need to thrive at school and giving every child the best start in life, whatever their background or wherever they grow up.

title: Coverage of Good Growth funding announcement

content.content: On Sunday (25 October), the government announced it will provide local leaders with £285 million to introduce Good Growth funding. This will give Mayors and local leaders more money, more powers, and more control, letting them invest in their priorities without seeking permission from Whitehall.

The funding could be used to bring the local high street back to life, improve essential transport links, or build new homes where they are needed.  Areas that are not yet strategic authorities will also be able to access a share of this money to support growth in their areas.

We also confirmed that we are working with Mayors to design a £1.5 billion borrowing facility from 2028, giving them access to capital needed to back their local priorities and deliver growth in every postcode.

There has been widespread coverage of the announcement in national media, including in The Guardian, Daily Mirror, Daily Express, Reuters, The Independent, andSky News, The HuffPost also featured an op-ed by the Prime Minister, focussed on the announcement. The announcement was also referenced in The Times and BBC News articles about the Budget.

The Secretary of State Angela Rayner appeared on the Sunday morning programmes, speaking about the benefits of the plans with Times Radio, LBC, ITN, Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg, Sky News’s Sunday Morning with Anne McElvoy
And there was further regional reporting by The Northern Echo, Manchester Evening News, Place Midlands, and Greatest Hits Radio.

Secretary of State for Housing, Communities and Local Government Angela Rayner said: “We’re putting a stop to mayors and local leaders being forced to come to Westminster cap in hand, asking for the power and funding that should rightfully be theirs.

“We’re backing our leaders to deliver what their communities need, from much-needed housing developments, stronger and better transport links, and the regeneration of the places people care so much about.
“That is what our devolution revolution really means – real decisions made locally, backed by real money, so every town and city can shape its own future.”

title: Behind the numbers

content.content: Tom Warth (Chief Operating Officer) talks about the human element behind planning as the latest performance statistics are published.
In the last couple of weeks two large solar farms were given development consent by the Government after independent examinations and recommendations by our inspectors.
Why do I mention that – we make thousands and thousands of decisions and recommendations a year after all?
No doubt it is good news for the applicants. Both schemes also contribute to the Government’s Plan for Change and the economic wellbeing of country.
But they also promise to generate enough renewable energy to power 380,000 homes – a decent size city. (See notes)

That’s real people in real homes and it’s a reminder that there are people’s lives behind every recommendation and decision we make and it’s why we make sure the same consideration, curiosity and quality go into each and every one.
Current performance
So how is that action translating into results? Well, our quarterly statistics have just been published and they tell us:

Some positive news there but that overall is not the same for every type of case. We know, in particular, that some enforcement appeals are taking considerably longer than we or our customers would like whilst some inquiries and hearings are being scheduled further ahead than expected. We’re working to improve this, but we also want to be realistic about the timescales customers may experience. You can see our latest published appeal timescales, including enforcement appeals, via this page on GOV.UK.

In the infrastructure world we've just completed the first 'acceptance' stage of an NSIP (Lighthouse Green Fuels) under the revised process following the Planning and Infrastructure Act bought in by the government to help drive an improved planning system. This is an example of how we are implementing Ministerial aims of streamlining the delivery of key national infrastructure.

In the plans service, we are preparing for a big increase in local plans examination as the ‘legacy’ system closes and the new plan-making system begins. Another example of the implementation of Government policy in which we play a key role.
Listening and acting

The data definitely tells us a lot and helps us shape our services, but we want more than the numbers. That’s why we value what you tell us about your own lived experience of the planning system and the services we provide.

There are lots of ways you can and do tell us, whether it be through the post-case surveys we issue, the chats we have at conferences, the questions and comments you provide in our webinars, or the responses you give in our stakeholder survey each year.

One thing that particularly pleased me in this year’s survey was the continued increase in those who responded to say they agreed or strongly agreed we have customer focus (39.6% in 2026 compared to 36.7% in 2025 and 31.1% in 2024). It’s not yet where we want it to be, but it is headed in the right direction.

We’re now around 18 months on from adopting a service model inside the Inspectorate which points all our resources towards supporting and improving the services we provide. Of course, there’s more to do but this is a good indication that this work is having a positive impact.
Quality and consistency
It was also encouraging that 69.8% of those who responded agreed or strongly agreed our decisions, recommendations and advice are of a high quality regardless of the outcome of a case.
But I do recognise a number of comments were concerned at a perceived lack of consistency in decision-making.

It may sound like a cliche, but we must always recognise no two cases are exactly alike so comparison can tricky. An Inspector will reach a decision based on the evidence before them in any individual appeal.

Importantly we undertake rigorous quality assurance of appeal decisions post-issue to ensure the quality of our decisions remains high and identify areas where that can be improved through continuous inspector learning and development. Your feedback helps us with this too.
Continuous improvements
I don’t think it’s an exaggeration to suggest we are in the middle of the most substantial period of digital transformation undertaken by the Inspectorate.

Over the last year, we have continued to make progress across multiple services that support local planning authorities, applicants, developers and communities, as well as transforming the internal systems used every day by our case officers, inspectors and specialist teams.
In appeals, we have continued to expand the functionality available through our digital appeals service.
In the National Infrastructure planning service, we have been redesigning how users access information and navigate our services, read our recent blog post from Operations Lead, Oliver Blower.

We are also preparing for major changes to support the new local plans system and have launched a new service that allows users to search and access Crown development applications more easily, improving transparency and making information available in a more accessible format.
That kind of seismic change doesn’t happen easily, and I’m not surprised some of you expressed some frustration in the stakeholder survey on the early usability of some new systems.

However, we don’t just introduce these changes and run, each one is continually tested and updated to make them the most user-friendly for you and help improve services for all. Your honest feedback is one of the key drivers for that improvement.
Customers should expect to see new features and smoother experiences via our digital services as we continue to iterate.

title: How waste sites are regulated: what the Environment Agency and operators are responsible for.

content.content: The Environment Agency is the main body in England responsible for making sure waste is regulated effectively. As the population grows and the climate changes, managing waste well is more important than ever for a sustainable future. Our rules help cut down on emissions and protect local communities from problems like bad smells, which can seriously affect people's lives.

Achieving this depends on two distinct roles working together. Waste site operators are responsible for running their sites safely and legally, day in, day out. Our job is to make sure they do in a way that protects the environment, through permits, inspections and enforcement when things go wrong.
Why waste regulation matters
Waste sites play an important role in managing the waste that households, businesses and public services produce every day.

If they are not managed properly, they can affect local communities and the environment. Problems can include pollution, odour, litter, noise, pests, fires and impacts on rivers, groundwater and wildlife.
That is why many waste activities, such as recycling, treating, storing and disposing of waste, require an environmental permit and are regulated by the Environment Agency.
What are waste site operators are responsible for?
The company or organisation that operates a waste site is responsible for complying with its environmental permit.
That includes:
Operators are responsible for these activities every day. The Environment Agency does not run waste sites and does not manage their operations on behalf of operators.
What does the Environment Agency do?
Our role is to regulate waste sites in England.
We do this by:
We focus our efforts on protecting people and the environment and making sure operators meet the standards required by law.
How environmental permits work
Environmental permits set out the conditions that operators must follow.
Some activities can operate under what are called “standard rules permits” which apply to common, lower-risk activities. Others need bespoke permits tailored to the specific site and risks involved.

Permit conditions are designed to protect local communities and the environment. They may include requirements to control odour, emissions, waste storage, site management and environmental monitoring.
What powers does the Environment Agency have?
We have a range of legal powers to respond when operators fail to meet their responsibilities.
Depending on the circumstances, we may:
Our response depends on the seriousness of the issue, the risks involved and the evidence available.
Why sites are not always closed immediately when there’s a problem
Environmental regulation operates within a legal framework. Decisions must be evidence-based and proportionate.

We need to establish the facts, assess risks, consider legal tests and follow due process. In some cases, urgent powers may be appropriate. In others, the most effective approach may be to require improvements while maintaining oversight.
That can be frustrating for communities experiencing impacts, but taking action that is lawful, proportionate and evidence-based is an important part of effective regulation.
What happens when a site becomes non-compliant?
When we identify problems at a site, our first priority is understanding the environmental risk.
We may inspect the site, review monitoring information, assess permit compliance and require the operator to take corrective action.
Some issues can be resolved quickly. Others are more complex and may require ongoing regulatory intervention.
Where operators repeatedly fail to comply, we escalate our response using formal enforcement powers.
What happens if a site is abandoned?

While any type of waste site may be abandoned by an operator, some are more challenging than others when this happens, with landfill sites presenting particular risks. When a landfill site is operating, the Environment Agency's role is to regulate the site and ensure that the operator complies with the conditions of its environmental permit. The operator is responsible for managing the site, controlling pollution risks, maintaining infrastructure, and carrying out closure and aftercare requirements.

Occasionally, a landfill site may be abandoned. This can happen when an operator ceases trading, enters insolvency, or is no longer able or willing to manage the site. Determining who is legally responsible for a site is complex and requires a case-by-case assessment. Abandoned landfill sites can also be complex in terms of the issues they present. These may include landfill gas emissions, odour, leachate management, impacts on groundwater or surface water, land stability issues, and the deterioration of site infrastructure.
The Environment Agency is not the owner or operator of an abandoned landfill site and does not automatically take over responsibility for running it.
When we are involved, the Environment Agency's primary focus is to remove the risk of  serious environmental  pollution that could arise from these issues.
Because every landfill site is different, decisions are made on a site-by-site basis.
How we prioritise our work
We regulate thousands of permitted activities across England.
We cannot treat every issue in exactly the same way. We prioritise our resources where they can have the greatest impact.
When deciding how to respond, we consider factors such as:
This risk-based approach helps us focus on the issues that matter most for people and the environment.
Working together to protect communities and the environment
Effective regulation depends on everyone playing their part.

Operators must meet their legal responsibilities. Communities help by reporting concerns and providing local intelligence. Our role is to regulate fairly, consistently and using the powers available to us.

We know that waste sites can have a real impact on people's day-to-day lives. That is why we focus our efforts on protecting communities and the environment, holding operators to account and taking action where it is needed.
You can find more information and links to our work regulating waste and waste sites in England on our Waste Hub

title: The Apprenticeship Penalty

content.content: Once in a while, research hits a sweet spot of relevance and timeliness, in tune with the direction of governmental policy. A recent example is SSAC’s occasional paper No. 27 ‘The influence of the social security system on educational and vocational decision-making at age 16’.

This research tested the Government’s declaration that all post-16 educational and vocational pathways are of equal value against how social security works in practice for households with a young person aged 16-18. In particular, the research examined the impact of a young person taking on an apprenticeship versus staying on in education on overall household income and its distribution.

We gathered evidence from young people whose parents were on Universal Credit (UC) or were care-experienced and held roundtable discussions with key stakeholders including those in schools and with researchers, local authorities, think tanks, academics and advice and other voluntary organisations. We also consulted with senior policy officials in the Department for Work and Pensions (DWP), Department for Education and HM Revenue and Customs, as well as visiting a Youth Hub. We met with organisations in Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland to draw comparisons with initiatives within the devolved administrations.

Building on this we modelled seven scenarios, drawing on the expertise of Citizens Advice and DWP. The scenarios examined the financial impact and distribution of household income as a result of staying in education or taking up an apprenticeship. The families modelled included those on median income and those relying on UC, two-parent and lone-parent households, those with a disabled child at home and those without a disability, all in private rented accommodation, and in addition a young person who had left home due to estrangement from family and was living in supported housing. The findings were stark where an apprenticeship was chosen. Unlike staying on in education, where the 16 -18-year-old remained part of the family benefit unit, apprenticeship income is retained by the young person and counter-balanced by a loss in social security income for the rest of the household. The loss varied from £17.25 to £332.92 a week depending on circumstances. The latter far outstripped the apprenticeship earnings and occurred when a disabled young person who was the only child of a lone parent took on an apprenticeship, resulting in the lone parent losing child benefit and UC elements, including child element and a work allowance. Even in more common scenarios, taking on an apprenticeship meant the reality of parents having to seek a substantial contribution from apprenticeship earnings to maintain financial equilibrium for the household.

Our research also raised wider issues of the distribution of household income and questions of being dependent or independent at ages 16-18 depending on choices made. The findings bore out what we heard in practice, with parents often not realising the ramifications for household income of the choice made to take on an apprenticeship. There was little evidence of good quality information being available to enable informed choices based on the social security impact of decisions made. Moreover, surviving the first month of an apprenticeship, with costs for travel, work clothes, equipment and other expenses having to be met until the first pay day, was prohibitively challenging. Care-leavers, estranged young people, young carers and those with disabilities faced particular barriers when making decisions at age 16, with limited support to manage the transition. All these groups are especially prone to becoming ‘Not in Education, Employment or Training’.

Elsewhere, the tracking of those who drop out of education varied across the UK. In Scotland there were legislative requirements to proactively follow those dropping out in real time, while Wales adopted an end of each term audit and England and Northern Ireland monitored on an annual basis. Estranged young people and young adult carers were not routinely identified and frequently missed when dropping out of education.

Among the report’s key conclusions was that the social security system was inadvertently penalising families when their children pursued apprenticeships. This struck a discordant note against the government objective to promote apprenticeships alongside other vocational pathways. In its formal response, the Department accepted the finding on apprenticeships and acted with alacrity, with the Secretary of State for Work and Pensions announcing a new bursary worth up to £4,500 to support young people from families in certain situations into apprenticeships as part of wider measures. The announcement referenced the SSAC research as a catalyst for the initiative. We, like many others, are now awaiting the forthcoming Milburn and Timms reports to see where the wider questions of the treatment of young people in the social security system will head next.

We are now working on two further occasional papers. First is an examination of the process for uprating benefits, thresholds and caps outside those with statutory requirements to do so. Second is an exploration of how social security effectively supports income realities and employment opportunities for those aged between 60 and state pension age.
Whether these capture the zeitgeist to the same extent as our work on the choices to be made on education and apprenticeships at age 16-18 remains to be seen.

Read the Secretary of State for Work and Pensions’ full response to our report here: Government response to SSAC Occasional Paper 27: The influence of the social security system on educational and vocational decision-making at age 16 - GOV.UK
